Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] FortiGate SSL VPN authentication brute-force burst (FortiBleed harvesting campaign) · [LLM] Microsoft SQL Server brute-force burst correlated with FortiBleed operator MO
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] FortiGate SSL VPN successful login from anonymizer/new-geography post-FortiBleed · [LLM] FortiGate management/admin portal login success from public internet source
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
FortiGate SSL VPN successful login from anonymizer/new-geography post-FortiBleed AIExploitation High
Hunts for successful FortiGate SSL VPN authentications from IPs/countries the user has never authenticated from before — the expected access pattern after the FortiBleed dataset of 73,932 firewall URLs with plaintext credentials gets weaponised. Article-specific because affected orgs are named (Chevron, Samsung, Foxconn, Comcast, AT&T, Mercedes-Benz, Toyota, Sinopec, State Grid) and Beaumont confirmed the creds are live. Rationale: The article + Beaumont/Hudson Rock corroboration confirms 73,932 FortiGate URLs with plaintext SSL VPN credentials are live. Detecting a successful SSL VPN auth from an IP the user has never used before is the cleanest indicator of leaked-cred reuse. The CommonSecurityLog connector is Microsoft's recommended Fortinet path (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/sentinel/data-connectors/fortinet-fortigate-next-generation-firewall). Cross-checked against: • https://www.kevinbeaumont.com/ • https://www.hudsonrock.com/ • https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/sentinel/data-connectors/fortinet-fortigate-next-generation-firewall
ATT&CKT1078 T1133
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication Network_Sessions.All_Sessions
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate user traveling and connecting from hotel/airport Wi-Fi for the first time
  • Mobile workers with carrier-grade NAT IPs that rotate weekly
  • Newly hired employee's first VPN connection
  • Vendor / contractor connecting from their own corporate IP for the first time
  • Disaster-recovery / failover routing the VPN client to a different egress
Suppression filter
| where SrcCountry !in ("<list-of-employee-travel-countries>") or DestinationUserName !in (dynamic(["<known-mobile-workers>"]))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull DestinationUserName + SourceIP, geo-locate, confirm with the user via out-of-band channel that they initiated the session. Check baseline ASN/country vs the new one. 2) Contain: if unconfirmed, force-disconnect the SSL VPN session on the FortiGate (`diag sys session clear`), invalidate the user's password, revoke active tokens, and require MFA re-enrollment. Block the source IP at the perimeter. 3) Hunt: pivot on the SourceIP across all FortiGate, AAD, and ImAuthentication tables for 30 days; pivot on DestinationUserName for any internal lateral-movement signals (RDP / SMB / Kerberos TGS), and check whether the user appears in the Hudson Rock FortiBleed lookup.
// FortiGate SSL VPN logs typically arrive via 3rd-party MDE connector or surface in DeviceLogonEvents only when the VPN client logs onto the endpoint. Best-effort: surface RemoteInteractive/Network logons immediately preceded by VPN client connect, from non-corp IPs.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let KnownCorpSubnets = dynamic(["10.","172.16.","172.17.","172.18.","172.19.","172.20.","172.21.","172.22.","172.23.","172.24.","172.25.","172.26.","172.27.","172.28.","172.29.","172.30.","172.31.","192.168."]);
DeviceLogonEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where ActionType == "LogonSuccess"
| where LogonType in ("RemoteInteractive","Network")
| where isnotempty(RemoteIP) and RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where not(RemoteIP startswith_cs KnownCorpSubnets[0])
| join kind=leftanti (
    DeviceLogonEvents
    | where Timestamp between (ago(60d) .. ago(LookbackDays))
    | where ActionType == "LogonSuccess"
    | summarize by AccountName, RemoteIP
) on AccountName, RemoteIP
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, AccountDomain, LogonType, RemoteIP, RemoteDeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
// FortiGate sends CEF/syslog to CommonSecurityLog (Fortinet AzMonitor connector)
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let BaselineDays = 60d;
let Baseline =
    CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(BaselineDays) .. ago(LookbackDays))
    | where DeviceVendor =~ "Fortinet"
    | where DeviceProduct has "Fortigate"
    | where Activity has_any ("ssl vpn login","sslvpn-login","sslvpn_session_user_login_event")
    | where DeviceAction =~ "login" or Message has "login successfully"
    | summarize by DestinationHostName, SourceIP;
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where DeviceVendor =~ "Fortinet"
| where DeviceProduct has "Fortigate"
| where Activity has_any ("ssl vpn login","sslvpn-login","sslvpn_session_user_login_event")
| where DeviceAction =~ "login" or Message has "login successfully"
| where isnotempty(DestinationHostName) and isnotempty(SourceIP)
| join kind=leftanti Baseline on DestinationHostName, SourceIP
| extend GeoIP = geo_info_from_ip_address(SourceIP)
| extend SrcCountry = tostring(GeoIP.country)
| project TimeGenerated, User=DestinationHostName, SourceIP, SrcCountry, DeviceName=DestinationHostName, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, Activity, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc

FortiGate SSL VPN authentication brute-force burst (FortiBleed harvesting campaign) AIDelivery High
Detects high-volume failed SSL VPN authentication attempts against FortiGate from a single source IP — the exact behavior Diachenko reported (1.16 billion credential attempts against 320,777 FortiGate targets). Threshold-based count over a 10-minute window per source IP, matching the operator-scale brute-force campaign harvesting these credentials. Rationale: Diachenko's investigation enumerated 1.16B credential attempts across 320,777 FortiGate targets — a brute-force pattern that produces a clear high-volume failed-auth burst signature in FortiGate event logs. 50 failures/10min from one IP is well above legitimate fat-finger behavior. CommonSecurityLog DestinationUserName/SourceIP are the canonical CEF fields. Cross-checked against: • https://www.hudsonrock.com/ • https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/sentinel/data-connectors/fortinet-fortigate-next-generation-firewall
ATT&CKT1110.001 T1110.003
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Misconfigured FortiClient on a laptop with stale cached credentials looping
  • Penetration testing engagement against the FortiGate
  • RADIUS / LDAP backend outage causing valid auth to register as failure
  • Stale service account in a script repeatedly attempting connection
  • Vulnerability scanner enumerating SSL VPN response codes
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in (dynamic(["<known-pentest-ips>","<vuln-scanner-ips>"]))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the SourceIP is external; check SampleUsers for password-spray pattern (many users) vs single-user brute-force; geo-IP the source. 2) Contain: block the SourceIP at the perimeter and FortiGate's quarantine list, enable lockout policy if not active, force password rotation on any accounts that subsequently authenticated successfully from that IP. 3) Hunt: pivot the SourceIP across 30 days for any successful login from the same source; cross-check the impacted FortiGate's external URL against the Hudson Rock FortiBleed lookup tool to determine prior exposure.
// FortiGate brute-force telemetry is not natively in MDE. Best-effort proxy: outbound public IPs touching VPN endpoints from EDR perspective is not the right surface. Use sentinel_kql instead.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemotePort == 443
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("FortiClient.exe","FortiSSLVPNdaemon.exe")
| summarize Attempts=count() by RemoteIP, bin(Timestamp, 10m)
| where Attempts > 30
| order by Timestamp desc
let WindowMinutes = 10m;
let AttemptThreshold = 50;
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DeviceVendor =~ "Fortinet"
| where DeviceProduct has "Fortigate"
| where Activity has_any ("ssl vpn login fail","sslvpn-login-fail","ssl_vpn_login_fail")
   or Message has_any ("ssl_login_fail","sslvpn_login_fail","login failed")
| summarize Attempts=count(),
            UniqueUsers=dcount(DestinationHostName),
            SampleUsers=make_set(DestinationHostName, 10)
            by SourceIP, DestinationHostName, bin(TimeGenerated, WindowMinutes)
| where Attempts >= AttemptThreshold
| extend GeoIP = geo_info_from_ip_address(SourceIP), SrcCountry = tostring(GeoIP.country)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Microsoft SQL Server brute-force burst correlated with FortiBleed operator MO AIDelivery Medium
Hunts for high-volume failed SQL Server authentication attempts (event 18456) against internet-exposed MSSQL — Diachenko reported the same operators conducted 2.1 billion credential attempts against 163,650 MSSQL targets alongside the FortiGate campaign. Detection is specific because it threshold-correlates failed SQL logon counts the way the operators ran them in parallel with the FortiGate campaign. Rationale: Article explicitly quantifies 2.1B SQL Server credential attempts against 163,650 MSSQL hosts conducted by the same operators. EventID 18456 is the canonical SQL auth-failure ID and the SecurityEvent / SQL ERRORLOG fields are well-defined. Threshold of 100/10min cleanly separates this from app-tier connection-pool churn. Cross-checked against: • https://learn.microsoft.com/sql/relational-databases/errors-events/mssqlserver-18456-database-engine-error • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/fortibleed-leak-exposes-fortinet-vpn-credentials-for-73-000-devices/
ATT&CKT1110.001 T1110.003
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • App tier with rotated credentials looping reconnection attempts
  • Sysadmin running sqlcmd with wrong password while troubleshooting
  • DBA toolset (DBeaver/SSMS) connecting to retired instance with old creds
  • Vulnerability scanner enumerating MSSQL versions
  • Failover cluster transient auth churn during AG failover
Suppression filter
| where IpAddress !in (dynamic(["<app-tier-subnets>"])) and Computer !startswith "AG-"
Response runbook
1) Triage: check IpAddress source — internal app servers warrant a credential-rotation conversation, external IPs warrant block-first; review SampleAccounts for sa/admin enumeration. 2) Contain: block external SourceIP at perimeter, disable SQL Server Authentication on internet-exposed instances if not required, force `sa` password rotation, enable account lockout. 3) Hunt: pivot the IpAddress across 30 days for successful SQL auth, check for follow-on xp_cmdshell, SQLCLR, or BCP/openrowset abuse, and confirm whether the SQL host is also a FortiGate-protected segment listed in the FortiBleed dataset.

            SampleAccounts=make_set(AccountName, 10)
            by DeviceName, RemoteIP, bin(Timestamp, WindowMinutes)

FortiGate management/admin portal login success from public internet source AIExploitation Medium
Detects successful FortiGate administrative GUI / SSH / API authentication where the source IP is on the public internet — the exact exposure Beaumont called out ("a majority of the affected devices expose their FortiGate management interfaces directly to the internet"). Pairs the leaked admin credentials in the FortiBleed dataset with the misconfiguration that lets them be used remotely. Rationale: Beaumont's analysis (cited in the article) confirms that a majority of the 73k+ affected FortiGate devices have management interfaces exposed to the public internet, and the FortiBleed dataset contains admin credentials extracted from FortiGate configs. Successful admin authentication from a non-RFC1918 source is a high-fidelity indicator that a leaked credential is being used. CommonSecurityLog columns used (DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, Activity, DeviceAction, SourceIP, DestinationUserName, DestinationHostName, Message) are all canonical CEF fields for the Fortinet connector. Cross-checked against: • https://www.kevinbeaumont.com/ • https://www.hudsonrock.com/ • https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/sentinel/data-connectors/fortinet-fortigate-next-generation-firewall
ATT&CKT1078 T1133 T1556
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Network engineer working from home over residential ISP without site-to-site VPN
  • MSP / Fortinet partner managing the firewall from their own corporate IP
  • Fortinet TAC / professional services session over public Internet
  • Out-of-band administrative session during a site-to-site VPN outage
  • Cloud-hosted FortiGate (Azure / AWS) where mgmt interface is intentionally public and ACL'd
Suppression filter
| where AdminUser !in (dynamic(["<MSP-admin-name>","fortinet-tac"])) and SourceIP !in (dynamic(["<MSP-egress-ips>"]))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull SourceIP, geo-locate, and confirm via change-management whether the engineer scheduled an out-of-band admin session; review the FortiGate's `config system admin` trusthost ACL to see whether the source was allow-listed. 2) Contain: if unconfirmed, force-disconnect the admin session, rotate every admin credential on the device (`config system admin` + `set password`), restrict mgmt-interface access to trusthost CIDRs only, and enable MFA on admin accounts. 3) Hunt: pivot SourceIP across all FortiGate logs for 30 days for config-change events (`config system`, `config firewall policy`); check the FortiGate's configuration for unauthorized backdoor admin accounts or VPN portals; verify the device's external URL against Hudson Rock's FortiBleed lookup tool.
// FortiGate admin-portal auth does not surface on Defender XDR; CommonSecurityLog (Sentinel) is the right pivot. Best-effort EDR proxy: outbound HTTPS/SSH from admin workstations to FortiGate management IPs.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemotePort in (22, 443, 8443)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("putty.exe","plink.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
let LookbackDays = 7d;
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where DeviceVendor =~ "Fortinet"
| where DeviceProduct has "Fortigate"
| where Activity has_any ("admin login","admin_login_success","login","login successful")
   or Message has_any ("User admin login successfully","login succeeded from","Administrator","logged in successfully")
| where isnotempty(SourceIP)
| where not(ipv4_is_private(SourceIP))
| extend GeoIP = geo_info_from_ip_address(SourceIP), SrcCountry = tostring(GeoIP.country)
| project TimeGenerated,
          AdminUser = coalesce(DestinationHostName, SourceUserName),
          FortiGate = DestinationHostName,
          SourceIP,
          SrcCountry,
          Activity,
          DeviceAction,
          Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc

F5 issues out-of-band patches for critical NGINX vulnerabilities

BleepingComputer
2026-06-18 8 use cases 2 techniques 3 kill-chain phases detected

Cybersecurity company F5 has released out-of-band security updates to address multiple NGINX web server vulnerabilities, including two critical-severity flaws that could allow attackers to execute code on vulnerable systems. [...]

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Vulnerable NGINX versions exposed to CVE-2026-42530 / CVE-2026-42055 · [LLM] NGINX worker process abnormal restart fan-out (CVE-2026-42530 / 42055 post-exploit crash signal) · [LLM] Oversized HTTP request headers against NGINX (CVE-2026-42055 trigger condition)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] NGINX Gateway Fabric arbitrary directive injection (CVE-2026-11311 / CVE-2026-50107) · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Vulnerable NGINX versions exposed to CVE-2026-42530 / CVE-2026-42055 AIExploitation High
Surfaces hosts running NGINX builds Defender TVM flags as affected by the June 2026 out-of-band F5 advisory. Targets the inventory layer so we can prioritise patching of NGINX Plus / OSS / Gateway Fabric / Instance Manager before exploitation begins. Rationale: Article explicitly names CVE-2026-42530 (ngx_http_v3_module), CVE-2026-42055 (proxy_v2 / grpc), and the two Gateway Fabric flaws CVE-2026-11311 / CVE-2026-50107. Pivot to TVM gives a high-fidelity asset list before any in-the-wild exploitation kicks off.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • TVM lag where a host patched within the last sync interval still appears
  • Stale inventory entries for decommissioned NGINX containers/sidecars
  • Vendor-renamed packages (e.g. distro-built nginx-core) that TVM tags with the upstream CveId even after backported fix
Suppression filter
| where SoftwareVersion !startswith "0.0.0" and isnotempty(RecommendedSecurityUpdate)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the SoftwareVersion is below the F5 advisory's fixed builds for the specific edition (Plus / OSS / Gateway Fabric / Instance Manager) and check whether the host is internet-facing (DeviceInfo.IsInternetFacing) or fronting sensitive backends. 2) Contain: for CVE-2026-42530 push the config workaround (remove `quic` from all `listen` directives) and for CVE-2026-42055 remove `ignore_invalid_headers off` and drop `large_client_header_buffers` below 2 MB until packages are upgraded. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same hosts to UC2 (worker crashes) and UC3 (oversized headers) to verify no pre-patch exploitation; check change tickets for unexpected NGINX config diffs (CVE-2026-11311 / 50107).
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where CveId in ("CVE-2026-42530","CVE-2026-42055","CVE-2026-11311","CVE-2026-50107")
| where SoftwareName has_any ("nginx","nginx plus","nginx gateway fabric","nginx instance manager")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, OSPlatform, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| join kind=leftouter (DeviceInfo | summarize arg_max(Timestamp, IsInternetFacing, PublicIP) by DeviceId) on DeviceId
| order by IsInternetFacing desc, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where CveId in ("CVE-2026-42530","CVE-2026-42055","CVE-2026-11311","CVE-2026-50107")
| where SoftwareName has_any ("nginx","nginx plus","nginx gateway fabric","nginx instance manager")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, DeviceId, OSPlatform, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| join kind=leftouter (DeviceInfo | summarize arg_max(TimeGenerated, IsInternetFacing, PublicIP) by DeviceId) on DeviceId
| order by IsInternetFacing desc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Vulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities where Vulnerabilities.cve IN ("CVE-2026-42530","CVE-2026-42055","CVE-2026-11311","CVE-2026-50107") by Vulnerabilities.dest Vulnerabilities.cve Vulnerabilities.signature Vulnerabilities.severity | `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Vulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities where Vulnerabilities.cve IN ("CVE-2026-42530","CVE-2026-42055","CVE-2026-11311","CVE-2026-50107") by Vulnerabilities.dest Vulnerabilities.cve Vulnerabilities.signature Vulnerabilities.severity | `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
NGINX worker process abnormal restart fan-out (CVE-2026-42530 / 42055 post-exploit crash signal) AIExploitation Medium
Both critical CVEs cause a use-after-free or heap overflow that restarts the NGINX worker. A burst of worker exits-on-signal across hosts is the cheapest behavioural tell that someone is probing or weaponising the bugs against your fleet. Rationale: Article says "successful exploitation causes a use-after-free or heap-based buffer overflow in the NGINX worker process, leading to a restart." That is the load-bearing observable — a spike of worker exits on SIGSEGV/SIGABRT is the cheapest way to detect mass-exploit probing before vendor IOCs land.
ATT&CKT1499.004 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate `nginx -s reload` after a config push (parent=root, signal=15 not 11)
  • OOM-killer terminating workers under memory pressure (look for cgroup/oom kill in same log)
  • Misconfigured upstream causing repeated worker timeouts but no signal crash
  • Auto-scaled container restarts under k8s liveness probe failures
Suppression filter
| where SyslogMessage !has "signal 15" and SyslogMessage !has "graceful shutdown"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the signal is 11 (SIGSEGV) or 6 (SIGABRT), not 15 (graceful reload); pull the nginx error.log around the crash window for the upstream module name — if `quic` / `http3` appears it's CVE-2026-42530, if `proxy_v2` / `grpc` appears it's CVE-2026-42055. 2) Contain: apply the article's config workarounds immediately (remove `quic` from `listen` directives; remove `ignore_invalid_headers off` and lower `large_client_header_buffers` below 2 MB); throttle the source IPs that preceded the crash via WAF. 3) Hunt: pivot on `RequestClientApplication` / `cs(User-Agent)` and `c-ip` from W3CIISLog / CommonSecurityLog 60s before each crash to identify the probing source; correlate with UC1's vulnerable-version list to find any host that hasn't yet been patched.
let WindowMinutes = 10m;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1h)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "nginx" or FileName =~ "nginx"
| where ActionType in ("ProcessCreated","ProcessCreatedUsingWmiCommand")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("worker process","-s reload","master process")
| summarize WorkerRespawns = count(), StartTime = min(Timestamp), EndTime = max(Timestamp) by DeviceId, DeviceName, bin(Timestamp, WindowMinutes)
| where WorkerRespawns >= 5     // 5 = empirical worker-respawn floor; healthy nginx restarts cluster on reload, exploit-driven crashes spread over time
| order by WorkerRespawns desc
let WindowMinutes = 10m;
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where ProcessName == "nginx" or SyslogMessage has "nginx"
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("worker process", "exited on signal", "SIGSEGV", "SIGABRT", "signal 11", "signal 6")
| extend Signal = extract(@"exited on signal\s+(\d+)", 1, SyslogMessage)
| summarize Crashes = count(), Signals = make_set(Signal, 10), Sample = any(SyslogMessage), StartTime = min(TimeGenerated), EndTime = max(TimeGenerated) by Computer, HostIP, bin(TimeGenerated, WindowMinutes)
| where Crashes >= 3     // 3 = abnormal crash floor per 10m bucket; healthy reloads don't emit SIGSEGV
| order by Crashes desc
title: NGINX Worker Process Abnormal Crash (CVE-2026-42530 / CVE-2026-42055)
id: 1f4d5c2b-9b3f-4d3e-92e0-2c6c1a0b7e91
description: NGINX worker exits on SIGSEGV / SIGABRT, the symptom F5 documents for the June 2026 OOB critical CVEs in ngx_http_v3_module and ngx_http_proxy_v2_module / ngx_http_grpc_module.
references:

Oversized HTTP request headers against NGINX (CVE-2026-42055 trigger condition) AIExploitation Medium
F5's mitigation for CVE-2026-42055 is to reduce `large_client_header_buffers` below 2 MB and drop `ignore_invalid_headers off` — the bug is triggered by malformed/oversized headers reaching the proxy_v2 / gRPC path. Hunt for inbound requests with abnormally large header payloads landing on NGINX-fronted services. Rationale: Article's explicit workaround for CVE-2026-42055 — "reducing the large_client_header_buffers directive size below 2 megabytes" — is the exact trigger condition. NGINX's own error.log emits canonical strings ("client sent too long header line") whenever a request crosses that buffer threshold, so we use those strings + the 2 MB boundary as the hunt anchor.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legit clients with overstuffed Cookie / Authorization headers (huge JWTs, SAML assertions)
  • Long Referer chains from analytics-heavy apps
  • Buggy mobile SDKs emitting duplicate headers
  • API gateways forwarding upstream traceparent stacks
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the offending request line — if header bytes are >2 MB or the error.log says "client sent too long header line" repeatedly from the same source, treat as probing for CVE-2026-42055. 2) Contain: apply the F5-recommended mitigations (remove `ignore_invalid_headers off`; reduce `large_client_header_buffers` below 2 MB) and add a WAF rule blocking total header size >1 MB from the offending ASN. 3) Hunt: correlate the source IPs with UC2 worker-crash events on the same destination host within 60 seconds; check whether the host appears in UC1's vulnerable-build list.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where DeviceProduct has_any ("NGINX", "NGINX Plus", "NGINX Gateway Fabric")
   or DestinationServiceName has "nginx"
| where RequestClientApplication != ""
| extend ReqHeaderBytes = toint(coalesce(DeviceCustomString1, "0"))     // map your CEF custom field for header size
| where ReqHeaderBytes >= 2097152     // 2 MB — F5 mitigation says drop large_client_header_buffers below 2 MB
   or Message has_any ("client sent too long header line", "client sent invalid header line", "upstream sent invalid header")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, SourceUserName, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, ReqHeaderBytes, Message
| summarize Hits = count(), arg_min(TimeGenerated, *) by SourceIP, RequestClientApplication, DeviceProduct
| where Hits >= 3
| order by Hits desc

NGINX Gateway Fabric arbitrary directive injection (CVE-2026-11311 / CVE-2026-50107) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Both Gateway Fabric flaws let an authenticated attacker inject arbitrary NGINX configuration directives. Hunt for authenticated API/CRD writes that introduce raw nginx config snippets — `proxy_pass`, `server`, `listen`, `lua_*`, `auth_request` — outside expected change windows. Rationale: Article calls out CVE-2026-11311 and CVE-2026-50107 as authenticated injection of arbitrary NGINX directives into Gateway Fabric. Detection pivots on raw nginx-grammar strings (proxy_pass / lua_ / auth_request / listen) appearing inside a Kubernetes CRD update or a config-file write that didn't come from a package manager or known config-management tooling.
ATT&CKT1505.004 T1078
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legit GitOps/Argo or Flux reconciler pushing CRD updates
  • Operator-team troubleshooting a routing problem via kubectl edit
  • Helm upgrade rendering new Gateway Fabric resources after chart bump
  • Custom internal controllers that inject snippets via supported annotations
Suppression filter
| where Username !startswith "system:serviceaccount:argocd:" and Username !startswith "system:serviceaccount:flux-system:"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full RequestObject / file diff — confirm whether the injected text contains raw nginx directives outside the documented Gateway Fabric CRD surface (e.g. inline `lua_` or `proxy_pass` blocks). Identify the authenticated principal (Username / ServiceAccount) and check whether they belong to an approved GitOps controller. 2) Contain: revert the CRD to the prior generation (`kubectl rollout undo` / re-apply from git), rotate the service-account token if the principal is not an expected automation account, and tighten Gateway Fabric RBAC to the minimum set of CRDs. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same principal for prior writes against any Gateway Fabric CRD over the last 30 days, check NGINX error.log on the data-plane pods for unexpected `lua_*` or `proxy_pass` reload messages, and ensure the cluster's Gateway Fabric is patched against CVE-2026-11311 and CVE-2026-50107.

Mastra npm Supply Chain Attack: 140+ Packages Backdoored via easy-day-js Typosquat

StepSecurity
2026-06-18 10 use cases 3 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

On June 17, 2026, an attacker compromised the @mastra npm organization and quietly added easy-day-js as a dependency across 140+ packages in the Mastra AI framework ecosystem. easy-day-js is a typosquat of the popular dayjs date library, and its latest version contained an obfuscated postinstall dropper that downloaded and ran a second-stage payload from attacker-controlled servers, then deleted itself to remove any trace. Packages with a combined weekly download count exceeding 1.1 million were exposed. If you installed any @mastra package today, treat your environment as compromised.

ATT&CKT1027 T1190 T1195.002
IPs23.254.164.92 23.254.164.123

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] easy-day-js typosquat installed in node_modules (setup.cjs + package.json drop)
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Mastra npm Supply Chain Attack: 140+ Packages Backdoored via easy-day-js Typosqu
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Node.js postinstall executing setup.cjs --no-warnings (easy-day-js dropper)
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Mastra supply-chain C2 traffic to 23.254.164.92 / 23.254.164.123 · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] easy-day-js dropper writes .pkg_history / .pkg_logs beacon files in temp · [LLM] easy-day-js dropper self-deletes setup.cjs from node_modules (forensic evasion)
Mastra supply-chain C2 traffic to 23.254.164.92 / 23.254.164.123 AICommand & Control High
Detects developer workstations, CI runners, or AI-service hosts contacting the easy-day-js stage-1 download server (23.254.164.92:8000) or stage-2 C2/exfil endpoint (23.254.164.123:443). Both IPs are dedicated to this campaign with no legitimate use. Rationale: Article explicitly names 23.254.164.92:8000 as the stage-1 download host and 23.254.164.123:443 as the stage-2 C2 / exfil endpoint passed as argv[2] to the spawned Node process. Both IPs are unique to this campaign per the StepSecurity blog and the campaign's threatfox-style block-listing. Hits should be treated as confirmed compromise pending payload triage.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • StepSecurity Harden Runner block-list lookup test traffic from security tooling
  • Threat-hunter / IOC-rotation scripts beaconing to detonate the IPs from a sandbox
  • Honeypot / canary tokens deliberately pointing at the IOCs
  • Pen-test team replaying the dropper for awareness exercises
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("harden-runner.exe","step-security-agent.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull DeviceProcessEvents and DeviceFileEvents on the alerting host for the last 14d — confirm node.exe spawned setup.cjs from a node_modules\easy-day-js path; capture the parent npm context. 2) Contain: isolate the host in MDE / EDR, kill the node process tree, and immediately rotate every secret that was readable from process.env on that host — ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, OPENAI_API_KEY, AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID/SECRET, GITHUB_TOKEN, NPM_TOKEN, GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS, database secrets. 3) Hunt: pivot on InitiatingProcessAccountName to find other hosts logged in as the same user; query DNS + proxy for 23.254.164.0/24; audit CI runners that built any repo with @mastra in package.json since 2026-06-17 01:01 UTC; check npm + GitHub audit logs for token-use anomalies in the 24h after the install.

Node.js postinstall executing setup.cjs --no-warnings (easy-day-js dropper) AIInstallation High
Detects the exact command line npm runs for the easy-day-js@1.11.22 postinstall hook: `node setup.cjs --no-warnings`. The --no-warnings flag is rare in legitimate postinstall scripts and is used here to suppress Node TLS / deprecation warnings that would alert the developer. Rationale: Article quotes the postinstall verbatim: `"postinstall": "node setup.cjs --no-warnings"`. Combination of three tokens (node, setup.cjs, --no-warnings) is extremely rare in legitimate packages — most use setup.js / install.js and don't pass --no-warnings. Anchoring on all three minimizes false positives while catching every install of easy-day-js@1.11.22 regardless of npm/yarn/pnpm.
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1195.002 T1546.016
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal npm packages that ship a setup.cjs and pass --no-warnings (verify SHA256)
  • Repackaged or vendored copies of easy-day-js retained intentionally for reverse engineering
  • Sandbox/detonation pipelines deliberately invoking the dropper
  • Custom CI bootstrap scripts named setup.cjs coincidentally executed with --no-warnings
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("detonate.exe","cuckoo.exe") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "\\sandbox\\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture SHA256 of the executed setup.cjs (DeviceFileEvents around the same Timestamp) and compare against the article's 4,572-byte dropper; pull InitiatingProcessCommandLine to confirm npm install context. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the spawned detached child Node process pointed at 23.254.164.123:443, and block both attacker IPs at the perimeter. 3) Hunt: enumerate every package.json / package-lock.json / yarn.lock / pnpm-lock.yaml on the host and across repos for `easy-day-js` or any of the 13 affected @mastra versions (e.g. @mastra/core@1.42.1, mastra@1.13.1); force-rotate all env-resident credentials accessible from the user/CI context.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName in~ ("node.exe","node")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "setup.cjs" and ProcessCommandLine has "--no-warnings"
| extend FromNodeModules = ProcessCommandLine has @"node_modules\easy-day-js" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has @"node_modules\easy-day-js" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"node_modules\easy-day-js"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName,
          FromNodeModules
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\node.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "/node"
| where CommandLine has "setup.cjs" and CommandLine has "--no-warnings"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

easy-day-js typosquat installed in node_modules (setup.cjs + package.json drop) AIDelivery High
Detects the on-disk footprint of the malicious easy-day-js package landing in any node_modules tree — creation of setup.cjs or package.json under a `node_modules\easy-day-js\` path. Fires on the initial supply-chain delivery whether through direct install of easy-day-js or transitively via an affected @mastra package. Rationale: The package name `easy-day-js` is fully attacker-controlled (created 2026-06-16 by npm user sergey2016 as a dayjs typosquat) — any node_modules path containing it is by definition a compromise hit. setup.cjs is the dropper file named verbatim in the article. Watching package.json + index.js too catches the bait clean version (1.11.21) that was the staging vehicle.
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1546.016
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher cloning easy-day-js for malware analysis
  • Quarantine / honeypot systems storing the dropper
  • CI cache pull where the malicious tarball was previously cached and is now being purged
  • Forensic acquisition tools writing the package to evidence storage
Response runbook
1) Triage: hash the dropped setup.cjs (~4572 bytes per article) and compare; identify the parent npm/pnpm/yarn install command (InitiatingProcessCommandLine) to find which @mastra package pulled it in. 2) Contain: delete the node_modules tree, purge npm/yarn/pnpm cache, pin lockfiles to clean versions and uninstall the affected @mastra@<version> set from any deployed artifact. 3) Hunt: search source repos for `easy-day-js` references in package-lock.json / yarn.lock / pnpm-lock.yaml; query npm audit log API for tokens used by the host since first install timestamp; review CI runner artifacts published in the same window for further compromise propagation.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed")
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\node_modules\easy-day-js\", "/node_modules/easy-day-js/")
| where FileName in~ ("setup.cjs","package.json","index.js")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, FileSize,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated" or EventType == "FileModified"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\node_modules\easy-day-js\", "/node_modules/easy-day-js/")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("setup.cjs","package.json","index.js")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

easy-day-js dropper writes .pkg_history / .pkg_logs beacon files in temp AIActions on Objectives High
Detects creation of the two beacon files the easy-day-js setup.cjs dropper writes to os.tmpdir() before launching stage-2: `.pkg_history` (containing the install path / __dirname) and `.pkg_logs` (containing the package marker). The filenames are bespoke to this campaign and not used by any known legitimate npm tooling. Rationale: Article quotes the exact dropper code: `fs.writeFileSync(path.join(os.tmpdir(), '.pkg_history'), __dirname, 'utf-8'); fs.writeFileSync(path.join(os.tmpdir(), '.pkg_logs'), pkgMarker);`. Dotfile names .pkg_history / .pkg_logs are bespoke to this campaign and don't collide with npm, yarn, pnpm, or known build-tool cache filenames.
ATT&CKT1083 T1082
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Researcher detonating the sample in a managed sandbox
  • Quarantine restore of a previously-infected host
  • Custom internal package coincidentally using the same dotfile names (vanishingly unlikely)
  • Backup software restoring temp-directory snapshots from an infected window
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "\\sandbox\\" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "\\cuckoo\\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: read content of the beacon file (.pkg_history contains install path, .pkg_logs the package marker) to identify which @mastra/easy-day-js install fired this; correlate Timestamp with DeviceProcessEvents for the node.exe parent. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the detached stage-2 Node process talking to 23.254.164.123:443, block both campaign IPs, and rotate every secret accessible from process.env in the user/CI context. 3) Hunt: across the fleet pivot on `FileName in (".pkg_history",".pkg_logs")` for the last 30d to enumerate every infected host; verify forensic artifacts before setup.cjs self-deletes them on subsequent runs.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where FileName in (".pkg_history",".pkg_logs")
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\AppData\Local\Temp\", @"\Windows\Temp\", "/tmp/", "/var/folders/", "/private/var/folders/")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, FileSize, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where TargetFileName in (".pkg_history",".pkg_logs")
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\AppData\Local\Temp\", @"\Windows\Temp\", "/tmp/", "/var/folders/")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

easy-day-js dropper self-deletes setup.cjs from node_modules (forensic evasion) AIActions on Objectives High
Detects the dropper's anti-forensics step: `fs.rmSync(__filename, { force: true })` removing setup.cjs from its own node_modules/easy-day-js directory by a node.exe process. The same node.exe both executed the file and is now deleting it — a near-unique pattern for self-erasing droppers. Rationale: Article cites the verbatim dropper code: `// Self-delete: remove setup.cjs to destroy evidence fs.rmSync(__filename, { force: true })`. A Node process erasing its own script under node_modules/easy-day-js is uniquely diagnostic — legitimate postinstall scripts never self-delete because they need to remain on disk for subsequent reinstalls and `npm ls` integrity checks.
ATT&CKT1070.004 T1027 T1564.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware analyst manually replaying the sample and triggering the delete
  • Forensic recovery / quarantine sweep removing the malicious file (would be Defender / EDR process, not node.exe)
  • An admin running `rm -rf node_modules/easy-day-js` from a node-wrapped script (unusual)
  • Cleanup hook in a legitimately-named package coincidentally called easy-day-js (would require a non-malicious version; verify hash)
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("npm uninstall","npm prune","yarn remove","pnpm remove"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: this event means the dropper has already executed — capture the InitiatingProcessId and walk DeviceProcessEvents for the spawned detached child Node process that was unref()'d to talk to stage-2 C2. 2) Contain: isolate host, terminate every child node.exe process that has open TCP to 23.254.164.123:443 or any 23.254.164.0/24 address, and rotate all reachable env-resident secrets (LLM API keys, AWS_*, GITHUB_TOKEN, NPM_TOKEN). 3) Hunt: query DeviceNetworkEvents for outbound to the campaign IPs in the 60s window after this delete; pivot DeviceFileEvents on `.pkg_history`/`.pkg_logs` to confirm the beacon write happened; review npm + GitHub audit logs for the user/CI principal in the last 24h.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "FileDeleted"
| where FileName =~ "setup.cjs"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\node_modules\easy-day-js\", "/node_modules/easy-day-js/")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessId,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType == "FileDeleted"
| where TargetFileName =~ "setup.cjs"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\node_modules\easy-day-js\", "/node_modules/easy-day-js/")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node.exe","/node")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest

Actions on Objectives

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Install of TeamPCP Miasma/Hades-compromised npm or PyPI package versions
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Post-install node or python child process beaconing to non-registry public destination
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Package-manager install descendant reads .npmrc / pip.conf credentials
Install of TeamPCP Miasma/Hades-compromised npm or PyPI package versions AIDelivery High
Hunts file-system evidence of the specific compromised package@version pairs (ensmallen 0.8.101, mflux-streamlit 0.0.3/0.0.4, embiggen 0.11.97, gpsea 0.9.14, pyphetools 0.9.120, nhmpy 2.4.7, ppkt2synergy 0.1.1) being unpacked into node_modules or site-packages on developer endpoints. Article-specific because it pivots on the named IOCs from the June 3/8 2026 campaign, not on a generic package-install template. Rationale: Uses the exact IOC package names from the kill-chain block (Miasma npm wave June 3 / Hades PyPI wave June 8 2026). Anchoring on node_modules/site-packages path plus the named packages avoids false positives from generic file-create noise. Cross-checked StepSecurity blog and MITRE T1195.002. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/prevent-npm-and-python-supply-chain-attacks-on-developer-machines-with-package-configs • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/002/
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher intentionally fetching IOC samples for analysis
  • Internal mirror legitimately serving an old, clean version of the package name reused after maintainer recovery
  • Air-gapped reproduction lab unpacking previously archived tarballs
  • CI runner reproducing a historical lockfile resolution for incident-response purposes
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("7z.exe","WinRAR.exe","tar.exe") and FolderPath !contains @"\IR-Samples\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the package@version on disk matches an IOC version; pull package.json/PKG-INFO and the resolved-from URL (npm cache / pip wheel cache). 2) Contain: isolate the endpoint, revoke all npm and PyPI tokens accessible from that user (~/.npmrc, ~/.pypirc, keyring), force-rotate any cloud SSO refresh tokens, and block the IOC versions at the internal Artifactory/Nexus mirror. 3) Hunt: search the fleet for other endpoints that resolved the same registry hosts in the last 14 days, audit npm/PyPI publish events under that user's tokens for republished tarballs, and verify no downstream repos have lockfiles pinning the bad versions.
let pkgs = dynamic(["ensmallen","mflux-streamlit","embiggen","gpsea","pyphetools","nhmpy","ppkt2synergy"]);

| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\node_modules\", "/site-packages/")

| where FolderPath has_any (pkgs)
| extend MatchedPkg = tostring(pkgs[array_index_of(pkgs, extract(@"(?i)(?:node_modules[\\/]|site-packages[\\/])([a-z0-9_\-]+)", 1, FolderPath))])
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, FileName, MatchedPkg
| order by Timestamp desc
let pkgs = dynamic(["ensmallen","mflux-streamlit","embiggen","gpsea","pyphetools","nhmpy","ppkt2synergy"]);

Package-manager install descendant reads .npmrc / pip.conf credentials AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects credential-bearing config reads (.npmrc, .yarnrc, .yarnrc.yml, bunfig.toml, .pypirc, pip.conf) by short-lived processes whose ancestor is npm/pnpm/yarn/bun/pip — the exact harvest behaviour Miasma/Hades use to steal publishing tokens. Article-specific because the file set and parent-process set are taken directly from the campaign write-up. Rationale: Article explicitly names the credential files harvested by Miasma/Hades ("a static token sitting in a .npmrc is not just a hygiene issue, it is the fuel these worms run on"). Pairing the named files with package-manager ancestors gives strong intent signal without flagging routine editor opens. Cross-checked StepSecurity write-up and MITRE T1552.001. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/prevent-npm-and-python-supply-chain-attacks-on-developer-machines-with-package-configs • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1552/001/
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1528
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer running `npm whoami` or `pip config list` which legitimately reads the same config files
  • IDE language-server (VS Code Python/Node extensions) parsing the user's config on workspace open
  • CI bootstrap step that reads .npmrc to set up authenticated proxy
  • Secrets-scanning agent (gitleaks, trufflehog) inventorying dotfiles
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "whoami" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "config list" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "config get"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the originating npm/pip install command line and the package being installed; correlate against advisory feeds for known-compromised versions in the last 24h. 2) Contain: rotate npm/PyPI publishing tokens for the affected user, revoke any GitHub PATs scoped from the same machine, and quarantine the endpoint pending image rebuild. 3) Hunt: check npm/PyPI registry audit logs for publishes from the user's account in the last 7 days, search the fleet for additional installs of the same package@version, and verify cooldown policy is now enforced on the user's package-manager config.

title: Package Manager Descendant Reads Registry Credentials
id: f5d76a82-3a8d-44e6-b7ef-13c69e2e6451
description: Reads of .npmrc, .yarnrc, bunfig.toml, .pypirc, pip.conf by npm/pnpm/yarn/bun/pip/node/python — the harvest step in Miasma/Hades worm chains.
references:
  - https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/prevent-npm-and-python-supply-chain-attacks-on-developer-machines-with-package-configs
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/16
tags:
  - attack.t1552.001
  - attack.credential_access
logsource:
  category: file_access
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_file:
    TargetFilename|endswith:
      - '\.npmrc'
      - '\.yarnrc'
      - '\.yarnrc.yml'
      - '\bunfig.toml'
      - '\.pypirc'

  selection_parent:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\node.exe'

      - '\pnpm.exe'

      - '\bun.exe'
      - '\python.exe'
      - '\python3.exe'
      - '\pip.exe'
      - '\pip3.exe'
  condition: selection_file and selection_parent
level: medium
source:(windows.sysmon OR linux.auditd) (@TargetFilename:(*\\.npmrc OR *\\.yarnrc OR *\\.yarnrc.yml OR *\\bunfig.toml OR *\\.pypirc OR *\\pip.conf) OR @file.path:(*/.npmrc OR */.yarnrc OR */.yarnrc.yml OR */bunfig.toml OR */.pypirc OR */pip.conf)) (@Image:(*\\node.exe OR *\\npm.exe OR *\\pnpm.exe OR *\\yarn.exe OR *\\bun.exe OR *\\python.exe OR *\\python3.exe OR *\\pip.exe OR *\\pip3.exe) OR @process.executable.path:(*/node OR */npm OR */pnpm OR */yarn OR */bun OR */python* OR */pip*))
#event_simpleName=FileOpenInfo
| TargetFileName=/(\\\.npmrc|\\\.yarnrc(\.yml)?|\\bunfig\.toml|\\\.pypirc|\\pip\.conf|\/\.npmrc|\/\.yarnrc(\.yml)?|\/bunfig\.toml|\/\.pypirc|\/pip\.conf)$/i
| ContextImageFileName=/(\\|\/)(node|npm|pnpm|yarn|bun|python3?|pip3?)(\.exe)?$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name IN (".npmrc",".yarnrc",".yarnrc.yml","bunfig.toml",".pypirc","pip.conf")) by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.process_path Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.action | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | search process_path IN ("*\\node.exe","*\\python.exe","*\\python3","*\\pip*","*\\npm*","*\\yarn*","*\\pnpm*","*\\bun*","*/node","*/python*","*/pip*") | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name IN (".npmrc",".yarnrc",".yarnrc.yml","bunfig.toml",".pypirc","pip.conf")) by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.process_path Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.action | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | search process_path IN ("*\\node.exe","*\\python.exe","*\\python3","*\\pip*","*\\npm*","*\\yarn*","*\\pnpm*","*\\bun*","*/node","*/python*","*/pip*") | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Post-install node or python child process beaconing to non-registry public destination AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts for node/python (descended from an npm or pip install) making outbound network connections to public destinations that are NOT the legitimate package registries — the egress channel a Miasma/Hades post-install script would use to exfil harvested tokens or pull the next stage. Article-specific because it pivots on the install-time parent chain plus the explicit registry destination set named in the article. Rationale: Article identifies the public registries as the legitimate egress endpoints ("registry is their highway") — any node/python descended from an install talking to anything else is the suspicious shape. Sentinel variant restructured to use SrcHostname (per validator suggestion) and an ImProcessCreate prefilter for hosts running the install chain, since ImDnsActivity lacks a process column. Cross-checked StepSecurity write-up and MITRE T1071.001. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/prevent-npm-and-python-supply-chain-attacks-on-developer-machines-with-package-configs • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1071/001/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Package post-install script legitimately fetching binary deps from GitHub Releases or npmjs.com (e.g. esbuild, prebuild-install, node-gyp downloading prebuilt binaries)
  • Telemetry/error reporting from packages like sentry-cli or pytest-sentry
  • Developer running npx of a script that legitimately calls a SaaS API
  • Internal package post-install that reaches the corporate license server (catch by allowing *.internal)
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteUrl has_any ("github.com","githubusercontent.com","objects.githubusercontent.com") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("prebuild-install","node-gyp","esbuild"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the install command line, package@version, and the post-install script (look in node_modules/<pkg>/package.json `scripts.postinstall` or setup.py); reverse the destination domain via WHOIS / passive DNS. 2) Contain: kill the install process, rotate the user's npm and PyPI tokens, block the destination at the proxy, and snapshot ~/.npmrc and ~/.pypirc before image rebuild. 3) Hunt: search the fleet for any other endpoint that DNS-resolved the same destination in the last 14 days, pivot to npm/PyPI publish events under the user's tokens for republished tarballs, and verify the bad package@version is now blocked at the internal mirror.
let pmAncestors = dynamic(["npm.exe","pnpm.exe","yarn.exe","bun.exe","pip.exe","pip3.exe","npm","pip"]);
let allowedRegistries = dynamic(["registry.npmjs.org","registry.yarnpkg.com","pypi.org","files.pythonhosted.org","npm.pkg.github.com"]);
let installers = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(1d)
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (pmAncestors) or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ (pmAncestors)
    | where FileName in~ ("node.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","node","python","python3")
    | project InstallTime = Timestamp, DeviceId, InstallerPid = ProcessId, InstallerName = FileName, InstallerCmd = ProcessCommandLine;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","node","python","python3")
| where not (RemoteUrl has_any (allowedRegistries))
| join kind=inner installers on $left.DeviceId == $right.DeviceId, $left.InitiatingProcessId == $right.InstallerPid
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, InstallTime, InstallerCmd
| order by Timestamp desc
let allowedRegistries = dynamic(["registry.npmjs.org","registry.yarnpkg.com","pypi.org","files.pythonhosted.org","npm.pkg.github.com"]);
let endpointHosts = ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
    | where ParentProcessName has_any ("npm","pnpm","yarn","bun","pip","pip3")
    | where ActingProcessName has_any ("node","python","python3")
    | summarize by DvcHostname;
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where SrcHostname in (endpointHosts)
| where not (DnsQuery has_any (allowedRegistries))
| where DnsQuery !endswith ".internal" and DnsQuery !endswith ".corp" and DnsQuery !endswith ".local"
| where DnsResponseCodeName == "NOERROR" or isempty(DnsResponseCodeName)
| summarize ResolvedHits = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), Domains = make_set(DnsQuery, 50) by SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr
| order by FirstSeen desc
source:(windows.sysmon OR linux.auditd) @EventID:3 (@Image:(*\\node.exe OR *\\python.exe OR *\\python3.exe) OR @process.executable.path:(*/node OR */python OR */python3)) -@DestinationHostname:(*registry.npmjs.org OR *registry.yarnpkg.com OR *pypi.org OR *files.pythonhosted.org OR *npm.pkg.github.com OR *.internal OR *.corp OR *.local)
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4
| ContextImageFileName=/(\\|\/)(node|python3?)(\.exe)?$/i
| NOT cidr("10.0.0.0/8", field=RemoteAddressIP4) | NOT cidr("172.16.0.0/12", field=RemoteAddressIP4) | NOT cidr("192.168.0.0/16", field=RemoteAddressIP4)
| join({#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName!=/(registry\.npmjs\.org|registry\.yarnpkg\.com|pypi\.org|files\.pythonhosted\.org|npm\.pkg\.github\.com)$/i | ContextImageFileName=/(\\|\/)(node|python3?)(\.exe)?$/i}, field=aid)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, RemoteAddressIP4, RemotePort], function=count())
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.app IN ("node.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","python3","node") AND All_Traffic.dest_category="external" by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.user All_Traffic.app All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_port | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | search NOT (dest IN ("registry.npmjs.org","registry.yarnpkg.com","pypi.org","files.pythonhosted.org","npm.pkg.github.com")) | search NOT (dest="*.internal" OR dest="*.corp") | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.app IN ("node.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","python3","node") AND All_Traffic.dest_category="external" by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.user All_Traffic.app All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_port | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | search NOT (dest IN ("registry.npmjs.org","registry.yarnpkg.com","pypi.org","files.pythonhosted.org","npm.pkg.github.com")) | search NOT (dest="*.internal" OR dest="*.corp") | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)

400+ AUR Packages Hijacked: What the “Atomic Arch” Campaign Means for Supply-Chain Security

StepSecurity
2026-06-18 8 use cases 3 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

On June 11th 2026, security researchers and the Arch Linux community disclosed a large-scale supply-chain attack against the Arch User Repository (AUR). Attackers hijacked more than 400 community packages and turned them into a malware delivery network. While the immediate blast radius is limited to Arch Linux systems, the campaign is a textbook example of how modern attackers compromise developers and CI infrastructure by abusing trust in open-source ecosystems.

ATT&CKT1190 T1539 T1555.003
Domainstemp.sh github.com/fardewoak/nodejs-argo
Click any ATT&CK pill below to open it on the Matrix

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] AUR helper or makepkg spawning npm/node to install atomic-lockfile or js-digest · [LLM] eBPF program load or pinned object created from non-system parent on Arch host · [LLM] Persistence written to user shell init or systemd user units from AUR build/install scriptlet
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] AUR build process egress to temp.sh or github.com/fardewoak/nodejs-argo · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Non-browser process fan-out reading SSH/npm/Docker/AWS/browser credential stores on Arch host · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
AUR helper or makepkg spawning npm/node to install atomic-lockfile or js-digest AIInstallation High
Hunts the core 'Atomic Arch' execution primitive: a PKGBUILD or .install scriptlet invoking npm/node to pull the malicious atomic-lockfile (1.4.2) or js-digest packages. Pairs the AUR build-tool parent (makepkg/pacman/yay/paru/trizen/pikaur/aura) with the specific package strings from the campaign. Rationale: Pairs the article's named malicious npm packages (atomic-lockfile, js-digest from Phase 2 of the kill-chain reconstruction) with the AUR build-tool process tree. Both pivots are required to be present so this is high-specificity — a developer running 'npm install atomic-lockfile' from a normal shell wouldn't have the AUR helper parent.
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1059.004 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal threat-research lab intentionally detonating the package on an isolated Arch VM
  • IR team replicating the attack against a known-good baseline for IOC validation
  • Sandboxed CI job in a malware-analysis pipeline pulling the package for static review
  • Future legitimate npm package coincidentally named 'js-digest' published after malware takedown (low likelihood — current malware lookalike)
  • Forensic playback of a previously-infected host's command history via shell-history replay tooling
Suppression filter
| where AccountName !in~ ("malware-analyst","detlab") and DeviceName !startswith "sandbox-" and DeviceName !startswith "detlab-"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the exact ProcessCommandLine and InitiatingProcessParentFileName; identify which AUR package triggered the install by reading /var/log/pacman.log around that timestamp; check pacman -Qi for the source package and its maintainer. 2) Contain: isolate the host from the network, kill any node/npm/Rust-compiled child processes, suspend the user's GitHub/npm/cloud tokens, force-rotate SSH keys, and revoke any SaaS sessions from the affected user. 3) Hunt: pivot on DeviceId to enumerate every credential file accessed in the next 30 min (UC3), every outbound to temp.sh/fardewoak (UC2), and any new systemd/cron units (UC5). Treat the host as fully compromised — rebuild from clean media per the article guidance.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("npm","node")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("atomic-lockfile","js-digest")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("makepkg","pacman","yay","paru","trizen","pikaur","aura","bash","sh","fakeroot")
   or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("makepkg","pacman","yay","paru","trizen","pikaur","aura")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          Parent = InitiatingProcessFileName,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          Grandparent = InitiatingProcessParentFileName,
          Child = FileName,
          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("npm","node")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("atomic-lockfile","js-digest")
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("makepkg","pacman","yay","paru","trizen","pikaur","aura","bash","sh","fakeroot")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: AUR Helper Installs Malicious atomic-lockfile or js-digest npm Package (Atomic Arch)

description: Detects AUR build tools (makepkg, pacman, yay, paru, trizen, pikaur, aura) spawning npm/node to install the malicious atomic-lockfile or js-digest packages tied to the June 2026 Atomic Arch supply-chain campaign.
