GentleKiller dropper executable in staging directory or AV-impersonating filename AIInstallation High
Detects execution of the standardized Gentlemen EDR-killer droppers — files named after the security product they impersonate (Kasps.exe, FaceIT*.exe, EAAntiCheat*.exe, BitD*.exe, Deletor.exe, HwAudKiller.exe, Symantec.exe, Sent.exe) and dropped from the 'GentlemenCollection' staging directory or user-writable paths. Combines naming convention with path constraint to suppress FPs from real AV binaries. Rationale: Dropper names (Kasps.exe, FaceIT*.exe, BitD*.exe, Deletor.exe, HwAudKiller.exe, Sent.exe, All.exe, buildx64.exe) and the 'GentlemenCollection' staging directory are explicit ESET findings. SHA-1 hash list (15 droppers) from the article is embedded for definitive hits. Path restriction to user-writable locations eliminates FPs from any legitimately-installed AV with similar names. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/gentlemen-ransomware-uses-multiple-edr-killers-to-disable-defenses/ • https://socradar.io/blog/dark-web-profile-the-gentlemen-ransomware/
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware researcher detonating an ESET-supplied sample bundle in a sandbox VM
  • Red team operator using publicly-leaked GentleKiller samples for an authorized assessment
  • DFIR analyst zipping these artifacts into a triage bundle (extraction event)
  • Legitimate FACEIT anti-cheat installer running from %TEMP% during game install — distinct because real FaceIT.exe is signed and runs from \Program Files\FACEIT\
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has "SANDBOX" or DeviceName has "MALWARE-VM" or DeviceName startswith "DFIR-")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("7z.exe","7zg.exe","winrar.exe","explorer.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm SHA1/SHA256 against the article's hash list. Note which AV vendor the binary impersonates — this hints at what's running on the host. Check parent process: was it RDP-spawned, dropped by a script, or extracted from an archive? 2) Contain: isolate the host immediately (these tools precede encryption by minutes), kill the process tree, block the SHA256, and look at the host's Defender / EDR-vendor service state — Gentlemen typically kills the EDR right before launching ransomware. 3) Hunt: pivot on the user account and source IP — look for the same SHA1 across the org, RDP logons from the same source, recent share enumeration (SMB/445), Volume Shadow Copy deletion (vssadmin), and ransomware encryption indicators (mass FileRenamed events).
let Droppers = dynamic(["kasps.exe","faceit1.exe","faceit2.exe","eaanticheatlight.exe","easolo2light.exe","easolo1clear.exe","bitd1.exe","bitd2.exe","deletor.exe","hwaudkiller.exe","sent.exe","all.exe","buildx64.exe","buildx641.exe"]);
let GentlemenHashes = dynamic([
  "8AE6BD18B129061F63642531F1B684CF0383C75D","D605994FC72A2BB59B5CFB1624A1B9170ECA73A2",
  "5AA3124E5C4921E5EDFC60133B5D71DA21B07DA3","331879F5EEC8892BBD896F90BDBB1BAD0BF63BD6",
  "F11AEBCCB9A86A7E2E653F90BAEC697F233C255F","EF9CD06683159397F099CAA244E94E6EAAD96EBA",
  "A11EE9CDC59E5CAA59AEFD27B30D104F3AD68E62","2F86898528C6CAB3540C486A9BFAA0C029B73950",
  "A19117175DBC9BA4D23B5DCE8415E299A2E32192","D29670E684E40DDC89B47010C37CBC96737035B6",
  "CF4D74DF17A91B4A36A2911B22AFEC5D8FA93A01","7131B377E96016DC1911020C9F95B1B4D042D7B4",
  "F0537CBB773AE12100B36731E7C39F5A9D852B14","A5CF917EC4A7DFBDFA43621398604805D860C718",
  "D4B19141102015D436321E6F26976E98183CFD27"]);
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where SHA1 in (GentlemenHashes)
   or FolderPath has "GentlemenCollection"
   or (tolower(FileName) in (Droppers) and FolderPath matches regex @"(?i)\\(Users\\Public|Temp|AppData|ProgramData|Windows\\Temp|Intel|PerfLogs)\\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA1, SHA256,
          ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,

let Droppers = dynamic(["kasps.exe","faceit1.exe","faceit2.exe","eaanticheatlight.exe","easolo2light.exe","easolo1clear.exe","bitd1.exe","bitd2.exe","deletor.exe","hwaudkiller.exe","sent.exe","all.exe","buildx64.exe","buildx641.exe"]);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| extend ExeName = tolower(tostring(split(NewProcessName, "\\")[-1]))
| where ExeName in (Droppers)
     or NewProcessName has "GentlemenCollection"
| where NewProcessName matches regex @"(?i)\\(Users\\Public|Temp|AppData|ProgramData|Windows\\Temp|Intel|PerfLogs|GentlemenCollection)\\"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName, SubjectUserName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Kernel-mode service registration for Gentlemen BYOVD drivers (Havoc service / %TEMP%\*.sys ImagePath) AIInstallation High
Detects registry writes that create or modify a Windows service whose ImagePath references a Gentlemen-associated driver, OR whose service name equals 'Havoc' (HavocKiller's hardcoded kernel service name per Huntress + ESET). Drivers loaded via SCM service must touch HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services — this is the registration step, complementary to UC1's file drop. Rationale: Huntress writeup explicitly notes the HavocKiller driver is registered as a kernel service named 'Havoc'. ESET names the driver filenames that get loaded — registering a service with ImagePath pointing at one of those drivers is the ring0-load step. The service-name match alone is very low FP (no benign software uses 'Havoc'), and the ImagePath match catches the file-drop-to-load chain. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/w2-malvertising-to-kernel-mode-edr-kill • https://thehackernews.com/2026/03/tax-search-ads-deliver-screenconnect.html
ATT&CKT1543.003 T1014 T1562.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate AV install (Safetica, Zemana, Qihoo 360) registering its own driver during MSI install — distinguishable by InitiatingProcessFileName=msiexec.exe + vendor-signed installer
  • Sysadmin manually copying a driver to %TEMP% for testing then using sc.exe create
  • Driver pack updater (Intel DSA, vendor utilities) registering an OEM driver under a non-standard service name
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msiexec.exe","trustedinstaller.exe","setup.exe") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("\\Temp\\", "\\AppData\\", "\\Public\\", "\\ProgramData\\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the InitiatingProcess that wrote the ImagePath — if it's not msiexec/TrustedInstaller/sc.exe from a signed installer, treat as malicious. Read the ImagePath, then look for the corresponding .sys on disk and hash it. 2) Contain: stop the service (`sc stop <name>`), delete the registry key, isolate the host. Note: if the driver is already loaded, only a reboot fully unloads it — schedule one. 3) Hunt: across the org, find every host with the same service name or ImagePath; pivot on the dropping process's parent to find the C2/RMM that delivered it; check for the Gentlemen dropper hashes from UC2.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryKeyCreated")
| where RegistryKey has @"\CurrentControlSet\Services\"
| where (RegistryValueName =~ "ImagePath"
         and RegistryValueData matches regex @"(?i)\\(eb|nseckrnl|stpm_old|stpm_new|dmx|360netmon_wfp|G11|googleApiUtil64|ThrottleBlood|havoc|IMFForceDelete)\.sys")
   or RegistryKey matches regex @"(?i)\\Services\\Havoc($|\\)"
   or (RegistryValueName =~ "ImagePath"
       and RegistryValueData matches regex @"(?i)\\(Temp|AppData|ProgramData|Users\\Public|GentlemenCollection)\\[^\\]+\.sys")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryKeyCreated")
| where RegistryKey has @"\CurrentControlSet\Services\"
| where (RegistryValue =~ "ImagePath"
         and RegistryValueData matches regex @"(?i)\\(eb|nseckrnl|stpm_old|stpm_new|dmx|360netmon_wfp|G11|googleApiUtil64|ThrottleBlood|havoc|IMFForceDelete)\.sys")
   or RegistryKey matches regex @"(?i)\\Services\\Havoc($|\\)"
   or (RegistryValue =~ "ImagePath"
       and RegistryValueData matches regex @"(?i)\\(Temp|AppData|ProgramData|Users\\Public|GentlemenCollection)\\[^\\]+\.sys")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Mass termination of EDR/AV processes by single non-system process (GentleKiller behavioral) AIActions on Objectives High
Detects a single user-space process killing 5+ distinct security-vendor processes from GentleKiller's 400-process target list within 5 minutes. The behavioral shape is the same regardless of which BYOVD variant is in play — kernel-driven termination of CrowdStrike, Defender, SentinelOne, Sophos, ESET, Kaspersky, Bitdefender, Trellix etc. is the unambiguous signal of an EDR-killer. Rationale: ESET documents 400+ processes across 48 security vendors targeted by GentleKiller — a single non-services.exe process terminating 5+ distinct EDR processes in 5 minutes has effectively no benign baseline. The behavioral threshold catches all GentleKiller variants regardless of which BYOVD is used, plus HexKiller/ThrottleBlood/HavocKiller, plus future variants. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/gentlemen-ransomware-uses-multiple-edr-killers-to-disable-defenses/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/03/54-edr-killers-use-byovd-to-exploit-34.html • https://www.huntress.com/blog/how-attackers-disable-av-edr
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1489
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT admin running an AV uninstaller script (CrowdStrike CsUninstallTool, Sophos UninstallCLI) during product migration — typically initiated by msiexec/TrustedInstaller and signed
  • Endpoint Detection rollout where a Defender-replacement product disables Defender during install
  • EDR self-update sequence that briefly cycles its services
  • Sysadmin running pskill / taskkill against AV during troubleshooting (rare)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !endswith "uninstaller.exe" and InitiatingProcessFileName !endswith "UninstallTool.exe" and InitiatingProcessFileName !has "CsUninstallTool" and InitiatingProcessFileName !has "UninstallCLI"
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("msiexec.exe","TrustedInstaller.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcess that did the killing; check its hash against the GentleKiller dropper list. If killer is unsigned, dropped to %TEMP%, or matches Gentlemen naming, treat as confirmed. 2) Contain: isolate the host (this is the last evasion step before encryption — minutes matter). Snapshot the disk if possible. Check VSS state — Gentlemen typically deletes shadow copies next. 3) Hunt: across the org, search for the same InitiatingProcess hash + the Gentlemen dropper hashes from UC2; check for the BYOVD driver drops from UC1; look for outbound C2 / file exfil from this host in the last 24h; correlate with any recent VPN / RDP logon from the same source IP.
let EDRTargets = dynamic([
  "msmpeng.exe","mssense.exe","securityhealthservice.exe","smartscreen.exe",
  "csfalconservice.exe","csfalcondaterepair.exe","csfalconcontainer.exe",
  "sentinelagentworker.exe","sentinelstaticengine.exe","sentinelagent.exe","sentinelhelperservice.exe",
  "sophosmtr.exe","sophoshealth.exe","sophosclean.exe","sophosfilescanner.exe",
  "avp.exe","klserver.exe","klnagent.exe",
  "bdagent.exe","bdservicehost.exe","vsserv.exe",
  "ekrn.exe","egui.exe","ecmd.exe",
  "mcshield.exe","masvc.exe","mfemms.exe",
  "avgsvc.exe","avgui.exe","avastsvc.exe","avastui.exe",
  "huntressagent.exe","huntressrio.exe",
  "carbonblack.exe","cb.exe","cybereason.exe","darktrace.exe",
  "traps.exe","cortex.exe","cyserver.exe",
  "tanium.exe","taniumclient.exe","threatlocker.exe",
  "deepinstinct.exe","diservice.exe","elastic-agent.exe","elastic-endpoint.exe"]);
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where ActionType == "ProcessTerminated" or ActionType == "ProcessKilled"
| where tolower(FileName) in (EDRTargets)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("services.exe","wininit.exe","system","taskhostw.exe","taskmgr.exe","msiexec.exe","trustedinstaller.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Temp\", @"\AppData\", @"\Public\", @"\ProgramData\", "GentlemenCollection")
| summarize KillCount = dcount(FileName),
            VictimProcesses = make_set(FileName, 50),
            FirstKill = min(Timestamp),
            LastKill = max(Timestamp)
          by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName,
             bin(Timestamp, 5m)
| where KillCount >= 5     // 5 distinct EDR/AV processes terminated in a 5-minute window
| order by FirstKill desc
let EDRTargets = dynamic([
  "msmpeng.exe","mssense.exe","securityhealthservice.exe",
  "csfalconservice.exe","csfalcondaterepair.exe",
  "sentinelagentworker.exe","sentinelstaticengine.exe","sentinelagent.exe",
  "sophosmtr.exe","sophoshealth.exe","sophosfilescanner.exe",
  "avp.exe","klserver.exe","bdagent.exe","bdservicehost.exe",
  "ekrn.exe","egui.exe","mcshield.exe","masvc.exe",
  "avgsvc.exe","avastsvc.exe","huntressagent.exe","cb.exe","cybereason.exe",
  "traps.exe","cortex.exe","tanium.exe","deepinstinct.exe","elastic-agent.exe"]);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where EventID == 4689   // process termination
| extend ExeName = tolower(tostring(split(ProcessName, "\\")[-1]))
| where ExeName in (EDRTargets)
| where ParentProcessName !endswith "services.exe" and ParentProcessName !endswith "wininit.exe"
| summarize KillCount = dcount(ExeName),
            VictimProcesses = make_set(ExeName, 50),
            FirstKill = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastKill  = max(TimeGenerated)
          by Computer, ParentProcessName, Account, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where KillCount >= 5
| order by FirstKill desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:5 @Image:(*\\MsMpEng.exe OR *\\MsSense.exe OR *\\CSFalconService.exe OR *\\csfalconservice.exe OR *\\SentinelAgentWorker.exe OR *\\SentinelAgent.exe OR *\\SophosMTR.exe OR *\\SophosHealth.exe OR *\\avp.exe OR *\\klserver.exe OR *\\bdagent.exe OR *\\bdservicehost.exe OR *\\ekrn.exe OR *\\egui.exe OR *\\mcshield.exe OR *\\avgsvc.exe OR *\\avastsvc.exe OR *\\HuntressAgent.exe OR *\\cybereason.exe OR *\\traps.exe OR *\\cortex.exe OR *\\elastic-agent.exe) NOT @ParentImage:(*\\services.exe OR *\\wininit.exe OR *\\msiexec.exe OR *\\TrustedInstaller.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ImageFileName=/\\(MsMpEng|MsSense|SecurityHealthService|CSFalconService|csfalcondaterepair|SentinelAgentWorker|SentinelStaticEngine|SentinelAgent|SophosMTR|SophosHealth|SophosFileScanner|avp|klserver|bdagent|bdservicehost|ekrn|egui|mcshield|masvc|avgsvc|avastsvc|HuntressAgent|cb|cybereason|darktrace|traps|cortex|tanium|deepinstinct|elastic-agent)\.exe$/i
| _eventType="ProcessTerminated" OR ProcessEndTime!=""
| NOT ParentBaseFileName=/^(services|wininit|TrustedInstaller|msiexec)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, bin(_time, 300000)], function=[count(field=ImageFileName, distinct=true, as=DistinctKilled), collect(ImageFileName)])
| DistinctKilled >= 5
ENDPOINT

| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process_name) as killed_processes dc(Processes.process_name) as distinct_killed from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.action="terminated" Processes.process_name IN ("MsMpEng.exe","MsSense.exe","SecurityHealthService.exe","CSFalconService.exe","csfalcondaterepair.exe","SentinelAgentWorker.exe","SentinelStaticEngine.exe","SentinelAgent.exe","SophosMTR.exe","SophosHealth.exe","SophosClean.exe","avp.exe","klserver.exe","bdagent.exe","bdservicehost.exe","ekrn.exe","egui.exe","mcshield.exe","masvc.exe","avgsvc.exe","avgui.exe","avastsvc.exe","avastui.exe","HuntressAgent.exe","CarbonBlack.exe","cb.exe","cybereason.exe","darktrace.exe") by Processes.dest Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process_path span=5m | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where distinct_killed >= 5 AND parent_process_name!="services.exe" AND parent_process_name!="wininit.exe" | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process_name) as killed_processes dc(Processes.process_name) as distinct_killed from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.action="terminated" Processes.process_name IN ("MsMpEng.exe","MsSense.exe","SecurityHealthService.exe","CSFalconService.exe","csfalcondaterepair.exe","SentinelAgentWorker.exe","SentinelStaticEngine.exe","SentinelAgent.exe","SophosMTR.exe","SophosHealth.exe","SophosClean.exe","avp.exe","klserver.exe","bdagent.exe","bdservicehost.exe","ekrn.exe","egui.exe","mcshield.exe","masvc.exe","avgsvc.exe","avgui.exe","avastsvc.exe","avastui.exe","HuntressAgent.exe","CarbonBlack.exe","cb.exe","cybereason.exe","darktrace.exe") by Processes.dest Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process_path span=5m | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where distinct_killed >= 5 AND parent_process_name!="services.exe" AND parent_process_name!="wininit.exe" | sort - lastTime
OxideHarvest credential stealer command-line pattern (-i hosts -u user -p pass -o output) AIActions on Objectives High
Detects the OxideHarvest credential-harvesting utility deployed by Gentlemen affiliates. The tool takes a distinctive flag combination (-i hostlist, -u user, -p password, -t threads, -o output) and pulls browser credentials from 25+ Chromium and Gecko browser profiles. Catches the binary regardless of rename via cmdline pattern. Rationale: ESET names OxideHarvest binary as buildx64.exe / buildx641.exe with SHA-1 hashes and documents its exact flag set (-i hostlist, -u user, -p pass, -t threads, -o output). The five-flag combination is extremely distinctive — almost no legitimate Windows tool uses this exact single-letter combination. Article-specific; not a generic browser-stealer template. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/gentlemen-ransomware-uses-multiple-edr-killers-to-disable-defenses/ • https://socradar.io/blog/dark-web-profile-the-gentlemen-ransomware/
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1003 T1078
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Open-source pentesting tools (impacket-style) with similar -i/-u/-p flag patterns — typically have additional positional args that distinguish
  • Internal automation scripts wrapping ssh/winrm with hostlist + creds + threadpool — narrow with whitelist of known internal tools
  • Custom homegrown admin utilities using single-letter flags (rare in modern enterprise tooling)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") or ProcessCommandLine !has "-Command"
| where ProcessCommandLine !has_any ("ssh ", "scp ", "rsync ", "curl ", "openssl ")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm SHA1 matches A5CF917EC4A7DFBDFA43621398604805D860C718 / D4B19141102015D436321E6F26976E98183CFD27, or inspect cmdline for the hostlist file (-i arg) — that file enumerates the next batch of targets. Pull and review it immediately. 2) Contain: isolate the host, capture the -o output file (contains harvested credentials), force-rotate every credential type the tool can extract (browser-saved passwords, cookies, autofill) for any user logged into this host in the last 30d. 3) Hunt: across the org, search for outbound transfers from this host (the harvested file is exfiltrated); look for the hostlist file's contents being touched by other infected hosts (lateral spread); pivot to identify the EDR-killer dropper from UC2 — credential theft typically follows EDR disable.
let OxideHashes = dynamic(["A5CF917EC4A7DFBDFA43621398604805D860C718", "D4B19141102015D436321E6F26976E98183CFD27"]);
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where SHA1 in (OxideHashes)
   or FileName in~ ("buildx64.exe","buildx641.exe")
   or (ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\s-i\s+\S+\.\S+"
       and ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\s-u\s+\S+"
       and ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\s-p\s+\S+"
       and ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\s-o\s+\S+"
       and ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\s-t\s+\d+")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath,
          ProcessCommandLine, SHA1, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| extend ExeName = tolower(tostring(split(NewProcessName, "\\")[-1]))
| where ExeName in ("buildx64.exe","buildx641.exe")
   or (CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\s-i\s+\S+"
       and CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\s-u\s+\S+"
       and CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\s-p\s+\S+"
       and CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\s-o\s+\S+"
       and CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\s-t\s+\d+")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName, SubjectUserName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Gentlemen OxideHarvest Credential Stealer Execution
id: 8e4a2b15-5d9c-4be4-cf45-3aa6ae1c5f44
status: experimental
description: Detects execution of the OxideHarvest credential stealer used by Gentlemen ransomware affiliates — matches by binary name (buildx64*.exe) or by the distinctive -i/-u/-p/-t/-o argument pattern.
references:
  - https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/killing-me-gently-inside-gentlemens-edr-killer-framework/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/19
tags:
  - attack.t1555.003
  - attack.t1003
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_name:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\buildx64.exe'
      - '\buildx641.exe'
  selection_args:
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - ' -i '
      - ' -u '
      - ' -p '
      - ' -t '
      - ' -o '
  condition: selection_name or selection_args
falsepositives:
  - Legitimate sysadmin utility with the same single-letter flag pattern (uncommon — most use long-form flags)
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 (@Image:(*\\buildx64.exe OR *\\buildx641.exe OR *\\BUILDX64.EXE) OR (@CommandLine:"* -i *" AND @CommandLine:"* -u *" AND @CommandLine:"* -p *" AND @CommandLine:"* -t *" AND @CommandLine:"* -o *"))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| (ImageFileName=/\\buildx64(1)?\.exe$/i
   OR (regex("\\s-i\\s+\\S+", field=CommandLine)
       AND regex("\\s-u\\s+\\S+", field=CommandLine)
       AND regex("\\s-p\\s+\\S+", field=CommandLine)
       AND regex("\\s-t\\s+\\d+", field=CommandLine)
       AND regex("\\s-o\\s+\\S+", field=CommandLine)))
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, SHA256HashData, ParentBaseFileName], function=[count(), min(_time)])
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as cmdline values(Processes.parent_process_name) as parent_process_name values(Processes.process_hash) as process_hash from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.user!="*$" (Processes.process_name IN ("buildx64.exe","buildx641.exe") OR (Processes.process="*-i *" AND Processes.process="*-u *" AND Processes.process="*-p *" AND Processes.process="*-o *" AND Processes.process="*-t *")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as cmdline values(Processes.parent_process_name) as parent_process_name values(Processes.process_hash) as process_hash from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.user!="*$" (Processes.process_name IN ("buildx64.exe","buildx641.exe") OR (Processes.process="*-i *" AND Processes.process="*-u *" AND Processes.process="*-p *" AND Processes.process="*-o *" AND Processes.process="*-t *")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | sort - lastTime
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("f7d335205b8d7b20208fb3ef93ee6dc817905dc3ae0c10a0b164f4e7d07121cd", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or SHA1 in~ ("f7d335205b8d7b20208fb3ef93ee6dc817905dc3ae0c10a0b164f4e7d07121cd", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or MD5 in~ ("f7d335205b8d7b20208fb3ef93ee6dc817905dc3ae0c10a0b164f4e7d07121cd", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("f7d335205b8d7b20208fb3ef93ee6dc817905dc3ae0c10a0b164f4e7d07121cd", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or SHA1 in~ ("f7d335205b8d7b20208fb3ef93ee6dc817905dc3ae0c10a0b164f4e7d07121cd", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or MD5 in~ ("f7d335205b8d7b20208fb3ef93ee6dc817905dc3ae0c10a0b164f4e7d07121cd", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["f7d335205b8d7b20208fb3ef93ee6dc817905dc3ae0c10a0b164f4e7d07121cd", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Mastra npm supply chain: easy-day-js postinstall dropper (node setup.cjs --no-warnings) AIInstallation High
Detects the easy-day-js@1.11.22 postinstall hook spawning the obfuscated setup.cjs dropper via Node.js with the --no-warnings flag. This is the entry point execution on any developer workstation or CI/CD runner that resolved the poisoned mastra/@mastra packages. Rationale: Anchors on the exact strings published by Microsoft for the malicious postinstall — node binary spawning setup.cjs with --no-warnings (Block 1 of the article). Also restricts the parent to npm/node/yarn/pnpm lineage to slash FPs from unrelated scripts that share the filename. Cross-referenced the mastra GitHub issue 18046 which confirms the postinstall hook in easy-day-js@1.11.22. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/mastra-ai/mastra/issues/18046 • https://www.linkedin.com/posts/microsoft-threat-intelligence_microsoft-has-identified-a-supply-chain-attack-activity
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1546.016 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate internal npm package whose postinstall is also named setup.cjs and invokes node --no-warnings (rare — the dual-string match makes this unlikely)
  • Developer manually testing/reverse-engineering the malicious dropper after the campaign was disclosed
  • A CI/CD job that intentionally runs a script literally called setup.cjs with warnings suppressed
  • Security tooling (EDR sandbox, npm audit replays) that re-executes the dropper for analysis
Suppression filter
| where SHA256 in~ ("b122a9873bedf145ae2a7fd024b5f309007dbb025149f4dc4ac3f7e4f32a36a4","c38954e85bf5433e61e7c8f4230336695624ae88b6953afabf7bf817aa91b638","cdec8b20338beb708b5be8d3d7a3041a35a8b0fb92f9186262f312d55ff82066","9570f77a5e1511869f4e554e7166df9fde081f2583e293c2569621792ed7d9c9","221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf") or FolderPath has @"\node_modules\easy-day-js\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full process tree on the host (parent npm/yarn → node setup.cjs); collect the SHA256 of the setup.cjs file and compare to the five published hashes; check $TMPDIR for .pkg_history and .pkg_logs markers. 2) Contain: isolate the host or CI runner from network, kill node tree, quarantine node_modules/easy-day-js, rotate every credential / token / SSH key / cloud key that touched that machine since 2026-06-16 07:05 UTC. 3) Hunt: query all hosts that ran npm install/update against the mastra or @mastra scope or that resolved easy-day-js@1.11.21 or 1.11.22 between 2026-06-16 and 2026-06-17; pivot to UC2/UC3/UC5 to confirm second-stage and persistence.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("node.exe","node")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "setup.cjs" and ProcessCommandLine has "--no-warnings"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm.exe","node.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","npm-cli.js","npm","node","yarn","pnpm","cmd.exe","powershell.exe")
   or ProcessCommandLine has_any (@"\easy-day-js\", "easy-day-js/setup.cjs")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| sort by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\node.exe"
| where CommandLine has "setup.cjs" and CommandLine has "--no-warnings"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, ProcessId
| sort by TimeGenerated desc
title: Mastra npm Supply Chain easy-day-js Postinstall Dropper
id: a1f8c3d4-7b2e-4f9a-8c5d-1e6b9f2a3c4d
status: experimental
description: Detects the easy-day-js@1.11.22 postinstall hook spawning the obfuscated setup.cjs dropper via Node.js with --no-warnings.

Mastra C2 beacon: node.exe to Hostwinds 23.254.164.92:8000 / .123:443 AICommand & Control Medium
Detects the setup.cjs dropper or its second-stage tasking client connecting to the attacker-controlled Hostwinds infrastructure used by the Mastra campaign. Single-event alerting on the two confirmed C2 IPs. Rationale: Two attacker-controlled IPs (23.254.164.92:8000 fetch, 23.254.164.123:443 beacon) and two Hostwinds DNS names published verbatim by Microsoft Threat Intelligence. Single-IOC match is high-fidelity because the IPs sit on a low-reputation hosting provider and were freshly stood up for this campaign. The DNS join catches detections even when the proxy resolves IPs locally. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/mastra-ai/mastra/issues/18046
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal threat-intel sandbox or red team detonating the dropper for research
  • Security researcher pivoting against the Hostwinds IP space from a corporate host
  • A different legitimate Hostwinds-hosted customer reusing the same IP after take-down (low — IPs were burned)
  • DNS scanner / passive DNS collector hitting the hwsrv-132778x hostnames
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","npm.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") or isempty(InitiatingProcessFileName)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process (expect node.exe), pull bytes-up/down to gauge whether the second-stage payload was retrieved or implant beacons completed; enrich the IP via passive DNS for any other Hostwinds C2 names. 2) Contain: block 23.254.164.0/24 at the egress proxy / firewall, sinkhole the two hwsrv-132778[56].hostwindsdns.com domains, isolate any host that connected. 3) Hunt: pivot on the source host to UC1 (setup.cjs execution), UC3 (NvmProtocal Run key), UC5 (wallet/browser data access); broaden lookback to 30d to catch any earlier connection from CI runners.
union
(DeviceNetworkEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
  | where RemoteIP in ("23.254.164.92","23.254.164.123")
  | where RemotePort in (8000, 443)
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256),
(DeviceEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
  | where ActionType == "DnsQueryResponse"
  | where AdditionalFields has_any ("hwsrv-1327785.hostwindsdns.com","hwsrv-1327786.hostwindsdns.com")
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, AdditionalFields, InitiatingProcessFileName)
| sort by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
(CommonSecurityLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
  | where DestinationIP in ("23.254.164.92","23.254.164.123")
  | project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, SourceIP, SourceHostName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication),
(DnsEvents
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
  | where Name in~ ("hwsrv-1327785.hostwindsdns.com","hwsrv-1327786.hostwindsdns.com")
  | project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType),
(ImNetworkSession
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
  | where DstIpAddr in ("23.254.164.92","23.254.164.123")
  | project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol)
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Mastra implant Windows persistence: NvmProtocal Run key + NodePackages drop AIInstallation High
Detects the cross-platform tasking implant installing login persistence on Windows by writing the NvmProtocal value under HKCU\...\CurrentVersion\Run and/or dropping protocal.cjs under C:\ProgramData\NodePackages\. Rationale: Microsoft Table 2 names the persistence artifact 'NvmProtocal' (note the typo — 'Protocal' vs 'Protocol') under C:\ProgramData\NodePackages\ — both strings are unique enough that any hit is essentially confirmed malicious. The typo is a high-fidelity anchor because legitimate NVM uses 'Protocol' or no such key at all. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/mastra-ai/mastra/issues/18046
ATT&CKT1547.001 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A user installs a legitimate NVM4W variant that coincidentally writes a similarly named key (extremely unlikely with the 'Protocal' typo)
  • Security tooling re-detonating the implant in an analysis VM
  • Forensic acquisition tooling reading the key (would show ActionType=RegistryQuery, not Set/Created — already filtered)
  • Manual analyst remediation activity touching the path after IR is underway
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("setup.exe","msiexec.exe") or RegistryValueData has "protocal.cjs"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the value data to confirm it points at protocal.cjs; correlate to the initiating process (expect node.exe, sometimes powershell.exe); hash protocal.cjs and compare against the published five SHA256s. 2) Contain: isolate the host, delete the Run value and the NodePackages folder, kill the implant process, rotate any credentials/tokens/cookies accessible to that user. 3) Hunt: query ImageLoadEvents / DllInjection for reflective .NET loads from node.exe in the prior 24h; check for the equivalent macOS LaunchAgent ~/Library/NodePackages/com.nvm.protocal.plist and Linux ~/.config/systemd/nvmconf/nvmconf.service across the fleet.
union
(DeviceRegistryEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
  | where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryKeyCreated")
  | where RegistryKey has @"\CurrentVersion\Run"
  | where RegistryValueName =~ "NvmProtocal"
        or RegistryValueData has_any (@"\ProgramData\NodePackages\", "protocal.cjs")
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName),
(DeviceFileEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
  | where FileName =~ "protocal.cjs" or FolderPath has @"\ProgramData\NodePackages\"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine)
| sort by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
(ImRegistryEvent
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
  | where RegistryKey has @"\CurrentVersion\Run"
  | where RegistryValue =~ "NvmProtocal" or RegistryValueData has_any (@"\ProgramData\NodePackages\", "protocal.cjs")
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine),
(ImFileEvent
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
  | where TargetFileName =~ "protocal.cjs" or TargetFilePath has @"\ProgramData\NodePackages\"
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileSHA256)
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Mastra implant credential access: node.exe reading crypto wallet extensions / browser History AIActions on Objectives High
Detects the second-stage tasking implant inventorying the 166 cryptocurrency wallet browser-extension IDs and copying browser History/Login Data into temp paths prefixed with 'browser-hist-'. Non-browser Node.js process touching browser profile data is the key signal. Rationale: Article confirms node.exe inventories 166 wallet extension IDs across Chrome/Edge/Brave profiles, copies History SQLite into temp paths prefixed 'browser-hist-' (verbatim). Non-browser process reading browser secret stores is normally rare; the node.exe-as-initiator pivot makes this a tight detection on developer endpoints.
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1005 T1217
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Electron-based developer tools (VS Code extensions, GitHub Desktop, Slack desktop) reading their own Chromium profile under User Data — distinguish via the Local Extension Settings/History/Login Data sub-paths
  • Browser-history exporters (e.g. browsing-history-export CLI) that some devs run via node
  • Backup/sync tools written in Node that snapshot the browser profile
  • Penetration-testing tooling on engagement laptops
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("Code.exe","code.exe","GitHubDesktop.exe","slack.exe","Teams.exe","Discord.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\AppData\Local\Programs\Microsoft VS Code\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the parent of node.exe (expect npm postinstall lineage from UC1, not VS Code / Electron); enumerate which extension IDs / which browser profile were touched; check for outbound POSTs to UC2 IPs within 5 minutes of the access. 2) Contain: isolate the host, terminate node tree, rotate seed phrases / hardware-wallet PINs / exchange API keys / 2FA seeds for every wallet found, expire all browser sessions for that user. 3) Hunt: correlate the user's Okta/Entra sign-ins and CEX exchange logins for the prior 7d; check for fund-movement events; pivot to UC2 for exfil confirmation and any HTTPS POST with the legacy IE8 User-Agent.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node")
| where (FolderPath has_any (@"\User Data\Default\Local Extension Settings\",
                              @"\User Data\Default\Extensions\",
                              @"\User Data\Default\History",
                              @"\User Data\Default\Login Data",
                              @"\User Data\Default\Cookies",
                              @"\Brave-Browser\User Data\",
                              @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\"))
   or FileName startswith "browser-hist-"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| sort by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ActingProcessName endswith "\\node.exe"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\User Data\Default\Local Extension Settings\",
                                  @"\User Data\Default\Extensions\",
                                  @"\User Data\Default\History",
                                  @"\User Data\Default\Login Data",
                                  @"\User Data\Default\Cookies")
   or TargetFileName startswith "browser-hist-"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @Image:(*\\node.exe OR *\\Node.exe) (@TargetFilename:(*\\User\ Data\\Default\\Local\ Extension\ Settings\\* OR *\\User\ Data\\Default\\Extensions\\* OR *\\User\ Data\\Default\\History* OR *\\User\ Data\\Default\\Login\ Data* OR *\\User\ Data\\Default\\Cookies*) OR @TargetFilename:*\\browser-hist-*)
#event_simpleName=FileOpenInfo ContextImageFileName=/\\node\.exe$/i (TargetFileName=/\\User Data\\.*\\(Local Extension Settings|Extensions|History|Login Data|Cookies)/i OR TargetFileName=/\\browser-hist-/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())

Mastra implant discovery: PowerShell child of node.exe running Get-StartApps / Get-AppxPackage AIActions on Objectives High
Detects the implant's host-fingerprinting step: enumerating installed software via Get-StartApps, Get-AppxPackage, and registry Uninstall keys in rapid succession spawned as a child of node.exe. Rationale: Microsoft's Phase 6 reconstruction names the exact three enumeration mechanisms (Get-StartApps, Get-AppxPackage, registry Uninstall) used by the implant for victim profiling. PowerShell as a child of node.exe is rare in normal developer use; combined with these three discovery commands, this is essentially confirmation of the implant being active.
ATT&CKT1518 T1518.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An npm package's postinstall that legitimately queries installed apps via PowerShell (rare but exists for some Windows-targeting npm modules)
  • node-based system inventory tools (e.g. systeminformation library wrappers) that shell out for AppX data
  • DevOps tooling that uses node to drive PowerShell-based Windows configuration checks
  • Electron app updater that queries Get-AppxPackage to detect Store-installed versions
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "systeminformation" and InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("electron.exe","Code.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full command line and parent node.exe command line; check if setup.cjs or a randomly named .js was the parent (UC1 lineage); look at the next 60 seconds of process events on the same host for follow-on PS reading browser data or registry hives. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill node and powershell trees, quarantine any .js dropped under temp/AppData. 3) Hunt: pivot on UC2 (C2 IPs) and UC5 (wallet/browser access) for the same DeviceId; check whether the user has any privileged AD / cloud roles and freeze them pending review.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Get-StartApps","Get-AppxPackage",@"\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| sort by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\node.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\powershell.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("Get-StartApps","Get-AppxPackage",@"\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["b122a9873bedf145ae2a7fd024b5f309007dbb025149f4dc4ac3f7e4f32a36a4", "c38954e85bf5433e61e7c8f4230336695624ae88b6953afabf7bf817aa91b638", "cdec8b20338beb708b5be8d3d7a3041a35a8b0fb92f9186262f312d55ff82066", "9570f77a5e1511869f4e554e7166df9fde081f2583e293c2569621792ed7d9c9", "221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Crypto Clipper uses Tor and worm-like propagation for persistence and control

Microsoft Security Blog
2026-06-17 12 use cases 15 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Microsoft Threat Intelligence analyzed a cryptocurrency clipper campaign that combines clipboard theft, wallet replacement, Tor-based communications, and worm-like propagation. Beyond stealing cryptocurrency transactions, the malware establishes persistent access and enables follow-on activity through a lightweight backdoor capability. The post Crypto Clipper uses Tor and worm-like propagation for persistence and control appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog .

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] CryptoBandits cfile payload artifact created under Public\Documents
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Crypto Clipper uses Tor and worm-like propagation for persistence and control
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] CryptoBandits scheduled task creation via XML import to Public\Documents 5-char staging folder · [LLM] WScript or CScript executing JavaScript payload from Public\Documents 5-char staging folder · [LLM] Renamed Tor client running as ugate.exe (CryptoBandits bundled proxy) · [LLM] Defender exclusion path added for Public\Documents staging folder (worm self-protection) · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Curl over Tor SOCKS5 proxy at localhost:9050 to .onion C2 · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] WScript or CScript with Public\Documents JS spawning curl, schtasks, cmd, or PowerShell child
CryptoBandits scheduled task creation via XML import to Public\Documents 5-char staging folder AIInstallation High
Detects the worm/stealer persistence step where schtasks.exe imports a task definition XML from a 5-character subfolder of C:\Users\Public\Documents. This is the exact persistence shape Microsoft published for CryptoBandits.A and is not produced by legitimate scheduled-task workflows. Rationale: Article code block 1 ships this exact regex verbatim — schtasks.exe + /create + /xml pointing into a [a-z]{4,6} subfolder of Public\Documents is the published CryptoBandits persistence signature and has effectively zero legitimate cause.
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1547
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Enterprise software-distribution tools that stage tasks via XML in Public\Documents (rare)
  • IT scripts that import scheduled tasks for shared workstations from a public staging share
  • Backup/imaging utilities that recreate scheduled tasks during post-deploy
  • Custom developer test harnesses validating schtasks /xml syntax
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("sccm.exe", "ccmexec.exe", "intunemanagementextension.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full ProcessCommandLine, the XML file at the referenced path (Defender DeviceFileEvents on FolderPath), and the parent that spawned schtasks.exe — a wscript.exe/cscript.exe parent is high confidence CryptoBandits. 2) Contain: isolate the device with MDE Live Response, terminate any ugate.exe / wscript.exe with parents in Public\Documents, and pull the XML + the JS payloads from the staging folder. 3) Hunt: pivot on the device for ugate.exe execution, curl with --socks5-hostname, cfile under Public\Documents, Defender exclusion adds, and look for the same 5-character folder pattern on other endpoints (USB worm spread).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "schtasks.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)schtasks\s+/create\s+/tn\s+[a-z]{4,6}\s+/xml\s+C:\\Users\\Public\\Documents\\[a-z]{4,6}\\[a-z]{4,6}\.xml\s+/f"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\schtasks.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)schtasks\s+/create\s+/tn\s+[a-z]{4,6}\s+/xml\s+C:\\Users\\Public\\Documents\\[a-z]{4,6}\\[a-z]{4,6}\.xml\s+/f"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: CryptoBandits Scheduled Task Import From Public Documents 5-char Folder
id: 6b9a4d1f-3c0e-4a2b-8e1a-cf2e3b6d9011
description: Detects schtasks.exe importing an XML task definition from a 5-6 character subfolder of C:\Users\Public\Documents, the persistence shape used by the CryptoBandits clipper worm.
references:
  - https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/crypto-clipper-uses-tor-worm-like-propagation-for-persistence-control/
author: thn-usecases
date: 2026/06/18
tags:
  - attack.persistence
  - attack.t1053.005
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith: '\schtasks.exe'
    CommandLine|re|i: 'schtasks\s+/create\s+/tn\s+[a-z]{4,6}\s+/xml\s+C:\\Users\\Public\\Documents\\[a-z]{4,6}\\[a-z]{4,6}\.xml\s+/f'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:(windows.sysmon OR windows.security) (@EventID:1 OR @EventID:4688) @Image:(*\schtasks.exe OR *\SCHTASKS.EXE) @CommandLine:(*"\\Users\\Public\\Documents\\"* AND *"/create"* AND *"/xml"* AND *".xml"*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\schtasks\.exe$/i
| CommandLine=/\\Users\\Public\\Documents\\[a-z]{4,6}\\[a-z]{4,6}\.xml/i
| CommandLine=/\/create/i
| CommandLine=/\/xml/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, CommandLine, ParentBaseFileName], function=count())

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name=schtasks.exe Processes.process="*\\Users\\Public\\Documents\\*" Processes.process="*/create*" Processes.process="*/xml*" by host Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process

| rex field=process "(?i)/tn\s+(?<task_name>[a-z]{4,6})\s+/xml\s+(?<xml_path>C:\\\\Users\\\\Public\\\\Documents\\\\[a-z]{4,6}\\\\[a-z]{4,6}\.xml)"
| where isnotnull(task_name) AND isnotnull(xml_path)
| convert ctime(firstTime), ctime(lastTime)
Curl over Tor SOCKS5 proxy at localhost:9050 to .onion C2 AICommand & Control High
Detects curl.exe being driven through the bundled Tor SOCKS5 proxy at 127.0.0.1:9050 with an .onion destination on the command line. This is the canonical C2 invocation shape for the CryptoBandits clipper /route.php, /recvf.php, and /stub.php endpoints. Rationale: Lifted from article code blocks 2 and 3 — curl.exe with --socks5-hostname localhost:9050 AND a .onion target on the same command line is unique to the malware's documented C2 flow; no legitimate Windows admin workflow co-locates these three tokens.
ATT&CKT1090.003 T1071.001 T1572
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Power user manually running a curl-over-Tor command to test the local SOCKS5 listener
  • Red-team C2 tooling using the same Tor SOCKS5 pattern in an authorised exercise
  • Researcher fetching darknet IOC feeds via local Tor client
  • Privacy-conscious user driving curl through Tor Browser's SOCKS port
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("tor.exe", "tor-browser.exe", "firefox.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull InitiatingProcessFileName — a wscript.exe/cscript.exe parent from C:\Users\Public\Documents is high confidence; capture the full .onion URL for IR notes. 2) Contain: isolate via MDE Live Response, kill curl.exe and any ugate.exe process, and block outbound 127.0.0.1:9050 path is moot — block the parent script and quarantine its folder. 3) Hunt: across the org look for ugate.exe, schtasks.exe importing XML from Public\Documents 5-char folders, cfile creation, and Defender exclusions for that path; treat any second host with the same 5-char folder name as part of the same USB-worm cluster.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "curl.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_all ("--socks5-hostname", "localhost:9050", ".onion")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\curl.exe"
| where CommandLine has_all ("--socks5-hostname", "localhost:9050", ".onion")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

WScript or CScript executing JavaScript payload from Public\Documents 5-char staging folder AIInstallation High
Detects wscript.exe or cscript.exe running a .js file inside the C:\Users\Public\Documents\<5char>\<5char>.js path layout the CryptoBandits worm drops. This is the runtime entry point for the clipper/stealer component that polls the Tor C2. Rationale: Article describes JS payloads dropped to C:\Users\Public\Documents\<5char>\<5char>.js (example given: 'omoho' folder) and executed by Windows Script Host; this combination of path and script host fires only on CryptoBandits-shaped activity.
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1218
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Endpoint-management agent dropping a one-off JS troubleshooting script to Public\Documents
  • MSP automation pushing .js fixes through a shared documents path
  • Custom in-house deployment tool using Public\Documents as a staging directory
  • Pentester or red-team operator simulating WSH-based persistence in the same path
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the .js file's SHA256 from DeviceFileEvents on FolderPath has 'Public\\Documents' and detonate in a sandbox or strings-scan for 'route.php', 'EVAL', 'SEED', 'PKEY'. 2) Contain: kill wscript.exe / cscript.exe with these arguments, quarantine the 5-char folder, and remove the matching scheduled tasks from UC1. 3) Hunt: pivot on the device for ugate.exe execution, curl --socks5-hostname, cfile drops, and the originating .lnk on removable media (DeviceFileEvents FileName endswith '.lnk' and FolderPath matches '^[D-Z]:\\').

| where FileName in~ ("wscript.exe", "cscript.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)C:\\Users\\Public\\Documents\\[a-z]{4,6}\\[a-z]{4,6}\.js"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\wscript.exe" or NewProcessName endswith @"\cscript.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)C:\\Users\\Public\\Documents\\[a-z]{4,6}\\[a-z]{4,6}\.js"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Renamed Tor client running as ugate.exe (CryptoBandits bundled proxy) AIInstallation High
Detects execution of a binary literally named ugate.exe — the article's exact name for the renamed Tor proxy that the clipper launches to bootstrap its hidden-service C2. Pair with the binary's location and parent to triage. Rationale: Article names the renamed Tor binary verbatim ('ugate.exe') and notes it is run hidden to bootstrap the hidden-service C2; no legitimate software ships an executable by this name.
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1090.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal app coincidentally named ugate.exe (very unlikely — verify FolderPath and SHA256 first)
  • Red-team operator simulating a renamed Tor client during an authorised test
  • Penetration-testing kit shipping Tor under the same masquerade name
  • Forensics or training lab analysing the same sample on a sanctioned VM
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "\\Users\\Public\\" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "\\AppData\\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull FolderPath, SHA256 and the parent process — a wscript.exe parent from Public\Documents is conclusive; submit the hash to the AV cloud and check Defender threat name for CryptoBandits.A. 2) Contain: isolate the device, terminate ugate.exe and its parent script host, and quarantine the binary plus the 5-char staging folder. 3) Hunt: search DeviceNetworkEvents for InitiatingProcessFileName == 'ugate.exe' to surface the C2, search across the org for the same SHA256, and check DeviceFileEvents for cfile and the JS payloads.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "ugate.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\ugate.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Defender exclusion path added for Public\Documents staging folder (worm self-protection) AIInstallation High
Detects the CryptoBandits worm's self-protection step where it adds a Microsoft Defender Antivirus exclusion for its C:\Users\Public\Documents staging path before dropping JavaScript payloads. Covers both PowerShell Add-MpPreference and direct registry writes to the Defender exclusion key. Rationale: Article highlights Behavior:Win64/PathExclusion.ST detections and describes the worm excluding its staging folder before dropping payloads; the path string 'Public\Documents' combined with Add/Set-MpPreference + ExclusionPath is article-specific.
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1112
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • MSP/RMM agent excluding Public\Documents because tenant uses it as a software-drop staging area
  • Sysadmin troubleshooting a Defender false positive on a shared workstation
  • Build farm or VDI gold-image script disabling AV scanning of staging directories
  • Endpoint security baseline tool reapplying a curated exclusion list
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("sccm.exe", "ccmexec.exe", "sense.exe", "intunemanagementextension.exe", "smc.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture InitiatingProcessFileName + parent chain — a wscript.exe / cmd.exe parent (not Intune/SCCM/admin shell) makes this CryptoBandits; check whether the exclusion is still active via 'Get-MpPreference | select ExclusionPath'. 2) Contain: remove the exclusion ('Remove-MpPreference -ExclusionPath ...'), isolate the host, and run a full Defender scan over Public\Documents. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC3 (wscript launching .js from the now-unexcluded path), UC4 (ugate.exe), and UC1 (schtasks XML import). Hash-collect anything new found under Public\Documents subfolders.
let ExclusionByPS = DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Add-MpPreference", "Set-MpPreference")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "ExclusionPath"
| where ProcessCommandLine has @"Public\Documents"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, Source = "PowerShell", Detail = ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine;
let ExclusionByRegistry = DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\Microsoft\Windows Defender\Exclusions\Paths"
| where RegistryValueName has @"\Users\Public\Documents\"
   or RegistryValueData has @"\Users\Public\Documents\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName = InitiatingProcessAccountName, Source = "Registry", Detail = strcat(RegistryValueName, " = ", RegistryValueData), InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine;
union ExclusionByPS, ExclusionByRegistry
| order by Timestamp desc
let ExclusionByPS = SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\powershell.exe" or NewProcessName endswith @"\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("Add-MpPreference", "Set-MpPreference")
| where CommandLine has "ExclusionPath"
| where CommandLine has @"Public\Documents"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, Source = "PowerShell", Detail = CommandLine, ParentProcessName;
let ExclusionByRegistry = ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\Microsoft\Windows Defender\Exclusions\Paths"
| where RegistryValue has @"\Users\Public\Documents\" or RegistryValueData has @"\Users\Public\Documents\"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer = DvcHostname, SubjectUserName = ActorUsername, Source = "Registry", Detail = strcat(RegistryValue, " = ", RegistryValueData), ParentProcessName = ActingProcessName;
union ExclusionByPS, ExclusionByRegistry
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CryptoBandits cfile payload artifact created under Public\Documents AIDelivery High
Detects creation of a file literally named cfile under C:\Users\Public\Documents — the article-specific artifact where the clipper stores attacker-supplied code downloaded from the Tor C2 /stub.php endpoint and later invoked via the EVAL command. Rationale: Article explicitly names the on-disk artifact: 'A file named "cfile" is created on the infected system as an output for payload hosted on the C2 domain' and ties it to the EVAL remote-code-execution path — high-fidelity host-side IOC for active EVAL tasking.
ATT&CKT1105 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer creating a file legitimately named cfile in Public\Documents (extremely rare)
  • Cross-platform configuration tool dropping a generic cfile artifact
  • Custom in-house script using cfile as a temporary write target
  • Forensic analyst restoring the sample during a sanctioned investigation
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture SHA256 and contents of cfile (it should be JScript) — strings-scan for ActiveXObject, WScript.Shell, eval; pull InitiatingProcessFileName to see which wscript.exe / ugate.exe-tied process wrote it. 2) Contain: isolate the host, terminate the writing process tree, and quarantine cfile plus the surrounding 5-char folder. 3) Hunt: this is evidence of an active EVAL session — search DeviceProcessEvents on the same host for any new child processes spawned by wscript.exe in the 60 minutes around the cfile write and treat anything novel as attacker-supplied code.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FileName =~ "cfile"
| where FolderPath has @"\Users\Public\Documents\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType =~ "FileCreated"
| where TargetFileName =~ "cfile"
| where TargetFilePath has @"\Users\Public\Documents\"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc
